title: H04 analysis preparation and provenance – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Sensitivity analyses The predefined branches change one aspect of the frame, weight, working variance, or placement while preserving the category estimand whenever that is possible. Exactly-one-category hours remove concurrent memberships. Retaining co-selected Other deliberately reverses the primary specificity rule. Excluding Other-only hours removes that varied display-only category, which is not a coherent scientific category. Unweighted long rows change the estimand by allowing multi-select hours to contribute more than one total unit. The placement-matched branch uses the same participants and participant-hours at the near-eye and chest sensor positions, then fits each position separately; it is not an equivalence or direct sensor-effect test. The remaining branches use the gap-timing-unaware dataset, change the working power to 1.30 or 1.80, or use the complementary chest position. The additional Mundlak-style branch retains the accepted long rows and 1/k weights. For every participant it calculates the weighted share of retained hours assigned to each of the five non-reference categories, then adds those five participant-level proportions to the additive site-plus-activity mean model. The current activity coefficients quantify category contrasts adjusted for usual participant composition. A between-participant coefficient is reported as the ratio for a 10 percentage-point higher usual category share, which corresponds to a lower At home share while the other shares are held fixed. Other remains unrestricted and display-only. The gap-timing-unaware dataset still requires at least 50% valid minutes per hour and at least 80% valid hours per day, but the timing of the remaining missing observations is not used for an additional metric-specific adjustment. At this first explanation only, the primary dataset could be interpreted as a time-sensitive primary metric dataset; hereafter it is called the primary dataset. title: H04 analysis preparation and provenance – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Weighted activity GAMs The exploratory nonlinear generalized additive model (GAM) analysis is separate from the primary population-mean inference. It allows the association with clock time to bend across the day, using the same long rows and exact 1/k weights with this exact formula: geo_medi_1h ~ s (time_hour, bs = "cc" , k = 12 ) + s (time_hour, activity, bs = "sz" , k = 12 ) + s (time_hour, site, bs = "sz" , k = 12 ) + s (time_hour, participant, bs = "fs" , k = 10 ) + s (participant_day, bs = "re" ) The global time smooth uses a cyclic cubic basis and joins across midnight. The activity and site sum-to-zero deviations use the approved thin-plate marginal basis and are not cyclic, so their fitted endpoints may separate at midnight. Participant-specific smooths and participant-day random intercepts remain in the fit. Activity-specific residual runs ensure that concurrent memberships at one timestamp never become lag neighbours. Show the R code used for this display temporal_basis |> transmute ( Component = recode ( .data $ component, ` global time ` = "Global time" , ` activity deviation ` = "Activity deviation" , ` site deviation ` = "Site deviation" ), ` Constructed class ` = .data $ constructed_class, ` Marginal basis ` = .data $ marginal_basis, ` Cyclic across midnight ` = if_else (.data $ cyclic, "Yes" , "No" ) ) |> gt :: gt () |> h04_gt () Table 28: Constructed smooth classes and midnight continuity. Component Constructed class Marginal basis Cyclic across midnight Global time cyclic.smooth cyclic cubic regression spline Yes Activity deviation sz.interaction tp.smooth.spec / tprs.smooth No Site deviation sz.interaction tp.smooth.spec / tprs.smooth No mgcv::bam() used a fixed-power Tweedie mean with log link, fREML, discrete computation, one R thread, and cyclic knots at 0 and 24 hours. A preliminary zero-correlation fit supplied the boundary-aware lag-one residual correlation; the final model used that value as its working AR(1) parameter. text: Population curves and uncertainty Displayed time/activity curves set participant and participant-day contributions to zero, evaluate every site observed at that sensor position, average those design rows equally on the fitted log-mean scale, and back-transform once to melEDI in lux. Their ribbons are model-based pointwise 95% CIs from the fitted coefficient covariance. A pointwise interval applies to one displayed clock time rather than to the entire curve simultaneously. Show the R code used for this display temporal_uncertainty |> transmute ( Placement = .data $ placement, Implementation = .data $ implementation, ` Interval type ` = .data $ interval_type, ` Covariance source ` = .data $ covariance_source, ` Critical value ` = .data $ interval_critical_value, ` Resampling replicates ` = .data $ resampling_replicates, ` Simultaneous band ` = if_else (.data $ simultaneous_band, "Yes" , "No" ), ` Curve-wide inference ` = if_else ( .data $ curve_wide_inference, "Yes" , "No" ) ) |> gt :: gt ( rowname_col = "Placement" ) |> gt :: fmt_number ( columns = ` Critical value ` , decimals = 2 ) |> gt :: fmt_integer ( columns = ` Resampling replicates ` ) |> h04_gt ( 9.8 ) Table 32: Recorded uncertainty construction for the exploratory temporal curves. Implementation Interval type Covariance source Critical value Resampling replicates Simultaneous band Curve-wide inference Near-eye H03-aligned fitted-coefficient covariance pointwise_95_percent_conditional stats::vcov(fit, unconditional = TRUE) 1.96 0 No No Chest H03-aligned fitted-coefficient covariance pointwise_95_percent_conditional stats::vcov(fit, unconditional = TRUE) 1.96 0 No No No bootstrap or simulation enters these curves. The intervals are not simultaneous bands, and no time-specific significant period or curve-wide inference is reported. Show the R code used for this display temporal_performance <- temporal_r_squared |> transmute ( Placement = .data $ placement, Quantity = "Participant-balanced raw-scale R²" , Value = .data $ r_squared ) |> bind_rows ( temporal_allocation |> transmute ( Placement = .data $ placement, Quantity = recode ( .data $ group, global_time = "Global time allocated share" , activity_deviations = "Activity-deviation allocated share" , site_deviations = "Site-deviation allocated share" , participant_curves = "Participant-curve allocated share" , participant_day_shifts = "Participant-day-shift allocated share" ), Value = .data $ shapley_share ) ) temporal_performance |> mutate ( Placement = factor ( .data $ Placement, levels = c ( "Near-eye" , "Chest" ) ) ) |> arrange (.data $ Placement, .data $ Quantity) |> gt :: gt ( groupname_col = "Placement" ) |> gt :: fmt_number ( columns = Value, decimals = 3 ) |> gt :: tab_source_note ( "The R² is on the raw melEDI scale with site-average and participant balance and 1/k within-hour weights. Allocated shares partition fitted natural-log predictor variance and are point summaries without uncertainty intervals." ) |> h04_gt () Table 33: Stored participant-balanced temporal-model performance and fitted-variance allocation. Quantity Value Near-eye Activity-deviation allocated share 0.307 Global time allocated share 0.525 Participant-balanced raw-scale R² 0.535 Participant-curve allocated share 0.084 Participant-day-shift allocated share 0.028 Site-deviation allocated share 0.056 Chest Activity-deviation allocated share 0.326 Global time allocated share 0.502 Participant-balanced raw-scale R² 0.500 Participant-curve allocated share 0.071 Participant-day-shift allocated share 0.035 Site-deviation allocated share 0.065 The R² is on the raw melEDI scale with site-average and participant balance and 1/k within-hour weights. Allocated shares partition fitted natural-log predictor variance and are point summaries without uncertainty intervals. The hierarchy-respecting Shapley allocation distributes shared fitted-model information across the temporal components rather than counting overlapping contributions more than once. It reports point estimates without uncertainty intervals. The remaining positive lag-one residual correlations mean that neighbouring hourly residuals are still related after the working AR(1) correction. The near-eye and chest results figures show the fitted activity curves, activity-to-global ratios, and effective weighted support. Their exact curve and support values are stored under artifacts/11_source_data/H04/ .

title: H05: Habitual light-related behaviour and personal light exposure – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Question The Light Exposure Behaviour Assessment (LEBA) asks about habitual light-related behaviours. The preregistered hypothesis was: “H5: LEBA questionnaire factors correlate with selected personal light exposure metrics.” This analysis tests whether four LEBA factor scores are associated with 17 personal light-exposure metrics after accounting for study site. Higher scores mean that the behaviour described by a factor was reported more often. Note Answer in brief None of the 68 primary near-eye associations remained statistically supported after false-discovery-rate (FDR) adjustment across the complete family, and the four planned sleep-environment cells are unfit for inference. The leading positive near-eye estimates remained descriptive, the complementary chest analysis reached the same family-wide conclusion, and the planned sensitivity analyses did not change that interpretation. Important model-check and site-influence limitations are summarized below.

title: H05: Habitual light-related behaviour and personal light exposure – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Orientation The four scores describe spending time outdoors (F2), devices in bed (F3), ambient light before bedtime (F4), and morning/daytime light use (F5). F2 includes one reverse-coded item; F3–F5 are sums of their ordered items. Every factor score was complete. Within each exact model sample, the score was centred and expressed both per raw point and per participant-level standard deviation. The report uses one participant-level SD so estimates can be compared across the four differently ranged factor scores. Near-eye measurements are primary because they more closely represent light near the eyes. All available chest measurements are analysed separately as complementary evidence and are not interpreted as ocular exposure. A participant-day is one eligible local calendar day from one participant; daily metrics can therefore contribute repeated days from the same person. A common-sample analysis fits the near-eye and chest models to the same participants and participant-days at both sensor positions, so separately fitted placement estimates are not confused with differences in who contributed data. This is neither an equivalence test nor a direct test of a placement effect, and the placements are never pooled as independent observations. The 95% confidence interval (CI) describes uncertainty around each reported effect. False-discovery-rate (FDR) adjustment limits the expected proportion of false discoveries across the complete planned family. The main models treat study site as a fixed effect, meaning that each study site receives its own adjustment. A random effect instead represents variation attributed to a grouping variable, such as participant or study site, rather than estimating a separate coefficient for each group. A sensitivity analysis repeats an accepted comparison under a predefined alternative to assess whether the interpretation is stable.

title: H05: Habitual light-related behaviour and personal light exposure – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
section: Model checks and the unfit sleep-environment boundary
text: Model checks and the unfit sleep-environment boundary Most near-eye and complementary chest models were acceptable or acceptable with specified limitations. The four sleep-environment cells at each placement are unfit for H05 inference because their simulated residuals and fitted response support show material failures. Their estimates, confidence intervals, and p-values are suppressed. This judgment applies only to the H05 response and model structure. It does not rule out analysing the underlying metric in another hypothesis with a different response variable, estimand, or model structure. A Tweedie model is a positive-response regression model that can accommodate right-skewed outcomes and exact zeros. For the sleep-environment outcome, that working model did not provide a defensible inferential representation. Show detailed near-eye model checks Figure 4: Near-eye model-check classifications for all 68 associations. Table 8: Near-eye model-adequacy counts. Models Acceptable 19 Acceptable with specified limitations 45 Unfit for inference 4 Table 9: Specified limitations identified by the near-eye model checks. Models Ordinary Gaussian residual warning 44 None specified 19 Unfit sleep-environment model: simulated-residual and response-support failure 4 Ordinary Tweedie simulation-based model-check warning 1 The model checks (model diagnostics) covered numerical fitting, residual behaviour, response support, and influence. All fixed-site fits completed, and all applicable Hessian checks were positive definite. That numerical completion does not make every response model scientifically defensible. Nineteen models were acceptable, 45 were acceptable with a specified limitation, and the four sleep-environment models were classified unfit for inference . Most retained limitations were ordinary Gaussian residual warnings. They qualify how closely the working residual distribution represents these data but do not indicate numerical fit failure. The following representative screens show F2 for the two leading estimates, the accepted MDER outcome, and the sleep-environment outcome. The smooth line in the residual-versus-fitted plot helps reveal fitted-dependent residual structure; the quantile plot compares standardized residuals with a normal reference. For the Tweedie sleep model, the simulation-based tests in the subsequent table, rather than the normal-reference plot, govern the assessment. section: H05 sleep-environment models are unfit for inference
text: H05 sleep-environment models are unfit for inference The four models for time below 1 lx melEDI during sleep require a stronger qualification than the ordinary residual warnings. Their simulated residuals showed pronounced non-uniformity, zero-mass disagreement, and outlier evidence. They also produced 183–187 fitted values above the participant-specific response support. These models are retained because the prespecified response-family assessment did not identify an adequate common replacement. They remain members of the complete planned family but are classified unfit for inference : their estimates, confidence intervals, and p-values are not used to support any scientific claim. This classification is specific to this H05 sleep-environment response and the model structure used here. It does not determine whether the underlying metric can be analysed in another hypothesis that uses a different response variable or model structure. text: MDER results and upper-tail checks A predefined sensitivity uses the gap-timing-unaware dataset . It applies the same general 50%-per-hour and 80%-per-day coverage rules, but does not use the timing of remaining missing observations for metric-specific adjustment. For this contrast only, the approved primary preparation could be interpreted as a time-sensitive primary metric dataset . Below, it is called simply the primary dataset. MDER is the arithmetic mean of viable one-minute melEDI/illuminance ratios. Both channels must be finite and strictly positive, and at least 720 of the complete 1,440 local wall-clock minutes must provide a viable ratio. Repeated local minutes on a daylight-saving fall-back day are averaged channel by channel before the ratio is formed; absent spring-forward minutes remain missing. Each viable minute ratio has equal weight, so MDER is not a ratio of daily integrals. Failure of this support rule makes only MDER missing. The gap-timing-unaware dataset left the family-wide conclusion unchanged; its exact 478-day MDER placement comparison retained all four directions with overlapping component intervals. No MDER association retained FDR-supported evidence. The small complementary chest coefficients were more sensitive to upper-tail observations, but their sensitivity intervals still crossed zero. Show MDER details and upper-tail checks MDER was available for 702 participant-days from 137 participants at all nine near-eye sites and 732 participant-days from 152 participants at eight chest sites in the primary dataset. In the gap-timing-unaware dataset, it was available for 687 near-eye days from 137 participants and 723 chest days from 152 participants. The exact paired/common gap comparison used 478 days from 107 participants at eight sites. The tables below give all four MDER associations in every accepted all-available and common-sample analysis. The all-available primary near-eye, primary chest, and gap-timing-unaware near-eye analyses retain their own complete 68-test families; common-sample rows are descriptive placement sensitivities. text: Site adjustment and site influence Fixed site was selected as primary because the inherited 17-metric site-structure evaluation fitted all fixed-site models successfully, whereas the corresponding random-site descriptions included two unstable, two non-estimable, and two singular fits. In the H05 sensitivity itself, 15 of 136 main all-available random-site fits were unstable: seven near eye and eight chest, while 121 passed. This instability is why random site is a sensitivity rather than the primary adjustment. Table 21: Random-site sensitivity fit status across near-eye and chest associations. Models Chest Fit passed 60 Fit unstable 8 Near eye Fit passed 61 Fit unstable 7 All 612 required leave-one-site-out refits completed. Twenty associations were stable, 27 retained direction but were magnitude-sensitive, and 21 changed direction after at least one site was omitted. The two leading F2 associations had no site-omission sign reversal and were classified stable. The broader pattern confirms that some small, near-zero estimates depend on which of the nine sites is represented, reinforcing the restrained family-wide interpretation. text: Gap-timing-unaware dataset The same model implementation was applied to the gap-timing-unaware dataset, including the same mean-of-viable-momentary-ratios MDER definition. This sensitivity gave no multiplicity-retained association; its smallest value was FDR-adjusted p = 0.070. Sixty-four of 68 estimates retained their sign and had overlapping component intervals; four changed sign, also with overlapping component intervals. The conclusion that zero associations retained FDR-adjusted support is unchanged. For MDER specifically, 687 near-eye days from 137 participants entered the near-eye sensitivity family, and its smallest MDER value was FDR-adjusted p = 0.107. The matched placement sensitivity used 478 days from 107 participants at eight sites; all four directions agreed and component intervals overlapped.

title: H05: Habitual light-related behaviour and personal light exposure – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Interpretation and limitations The strongest defensible conclusion is that, after fixed-site adjustment and one complete 68-test FDR adjustment, these data provide no multiplicity-retained evidence that any of the four LEBA factors is associated with the 17 selected personal light-exposure metrics. The positive F2 estimates for time above 1,000 lx melEDI and melEDI dose are consistent across the principal stability checks. Their confidence intervals describe non-zero associations before multiplicity adjustment, but their adjusted values do not support confirmatory claims. They should be treated as descriptive patterns that may motivate future work, not as established effects of spending time outdoors. This is an observational association analysis. LEBA scores are self-reported, site adjustment cannot remove all person-level confounding, only nine sites contribute to the primary analysis, and several small estimates are sensitive to site omission. Near-eye and chest measurements also represent related but non-identical light fields. Finally, the sleep-environment Tweedie models are unfit for inference because of material response-support and simulated-residual failures; their estimates and p-values are suppressed from the reader-facing results and cannot support a claim in H05. This judgment is specific to the response variable and model structure used here and does not preclude analysing the metric in another hypothesis with a different response or model. Uncertainty remains: several small estimates changed direction when a site was omitted, the small complementary chest MDER coefficients were sensitive to upper-tail observations but retained zero-crossing sensitivity intervals, and the four planned sleep-environment models are unfit for H05 inference under this response definition and model structure.

text: Models, response specifications, and inference For participant-day outcomes, the full model asks whether LEBA improves the site-adjusted description while accounting for repeated days from the same participant. Its participant random effect represents remaining between-participant variation after LEBA and site are considered. The reduced model removes only LEBA. Interdaily stability (IS) and intradaily variability (IV) have one response per participant, so they do not use a participant random effect. Fixed site effects use the registered site order and sum-to-zero contrasts; the LEBA coefficient is therefore adjusted for site without being tied to one reference site. This adjustment describes site differences and does not imply that site causes an exposure outcome. The registered random-site structure is retained as a sensitivity analysis. The following evaluated cell reads and prints the exact formula objects used for the full, reduced, and registered random-site sensitivity models. registered_formula <- function (analysis_unit, formula_id) { row <- formula_registry |> dplyr :: filter ( .data $ analysis_unit == .env $ analysis_unit, .data $ formula_id == .env $ formula_id ) stopifnot ( nrow (row) == 1 L) stats :: as.formula (row $ formula[[ 1 L]]) } h05_formulas <- list ( participant_day_full = registered_formula ( "participant_day" , "fixed_full" ), participant_day_reduced = registered_formula ( "participant_day" , "fixed_reduced" ), participant_full = registered_formula ( "participant" , "fixed_full" ), participant_reduced = registered_formula ( "participant" , "fixed_reduced" ), participant_day_random_site = registered_formula ( "participant_day" , "random_site" ), participant_random_site = registered_formula ( "participant" , "random_site" ) ) tibble :: tibble ( Model = c ( "Participant-day primary full" , "Participant-day primary reduced" , "Participant primary full" , "Participant primary reduced" , "Participant-day random-site sensitivity" , "Participant random-site sensitivity" ), ` Exact Wilkinson formula ` = paste0 ( "`" , vapply (h05_formulas, deparse1, character ( 1 )), "`" ) ) |> gt :: gt ( rowname_col = "Model" ) |> gt :: fmt_markdown ( columns = ` Exact Wilkinson formula ` ) |> gt :: cols_width ( ` Exact Wilkinson formula ` ~ gt :: pct ( 67 )) |> gt :: tab_source_note ( source_note = paste ( "The table is evaluated directly from the registered formula objects;" , "the reduced model removes only LEBA from the corresponding full model." ) ) |> h05_gt ( 12 ) Table 27: Exact evaluated formulas supplied to the H05 full, reduced, and random-site sensitivity models. Exact Wilkinson formula Participant-day primary full response_value ~ site + leba_centered + (1 | participant_key) Participant-day primary reduced response_value ~ site + (1 | participant_key) Participant primary full response_value ~ site + leba_centered Participant primary reduced response_value ~ site Participant-day random-site sensitivity response_value ~ leba_centered + (1 | site) + (1 | participant_key) Participant random-site sensitivity response_value ~ leba_centered + (1 | site) The table is evaluated directly from the registered formula objects; the reduced model removes only LEBA from the corresponding full model. Gaussian full and reduced models were compared using maximum likelihood. Tweedie models used a log link and maximum likelihood. Effects are back-transformed from the fitted scale to a practical response scale: a ratio for log-scale and Tweedie outcomes, an odds ratio for IS, a difference in the stated metric unit for identity-scale outcomes, and an hours difference for clock-time outcomes. text: Deviations and operational clarifications The preregistration gives the broad model Metric ~ LEBA + (1|Site) but does not fully define the repeated-measure structure, response families, metric set, multiplicity family, clock handling, or placement roles. The following choices make those elements explicit. Table 29: H05 model and inferential changes or operational clarifications. Preregistered or unspecified Analysed Why it matters Site adjustment Random site intercept Country-coded study-site-order fixed site effects; registered random-site model retained as a sensitivity The fixed-site structure was more reliably estimable with nine sites. Repeated observations Not operationally specified Participant-day responses for 15 metrics with a participant random intercept; participant responses for IS and IV Daily information is retained without treating days from one person as independent. Response model Generic linear model Metric-specific Gaussian or Tweedie model and approved response transform The outcome scale and support differ across the 17 metrics. LEBA scale Not specified Centred score; effects reported per one participant-level SD This retains the continuous score while giving a comparable effect unit. Inference and multiplicity Correlation matrices plus linear models; adjustment family not operationalized Full-versus-reduced LEBA comparison and one complete 68-test FDR family per inferential placement/scenario All four factors and 17 metrics remain in the correction. Table 30: H05 metric, clock, placement, and descriptive-output clarifications. Preregistered or unspecified Analysed Why it matters Metric set Selected metrics not enumerated Seventeen prespecified metrics, including corrected dose and MDER as the arithmetic mean of viable one-minute melEDI/illuminance ratios; both channels must be finite and positive, and at least 720 of the complete 1,440 local wall-clock minutes must be viable The 17 × 4 cross-product fixes the 68 tests before inference. Primary placement Not specified in H5 All-available near eye primary; all-available chest complementary; common-sample placements as sensitivity Separates the scientific measurement role from sample composition. Clock outcomes Not operationally specified Continuous supported ranges; darkest-10-hour midpoint values strictly after 16:00 are shifted to the preceding clock scale Avoids averaging across an artificial midnight discontinuity. Numerical zeros in darkest-10-hour mean melEDI Not operationally specified A geometric-mean back-transformation residual within the unit-aware floating-point tolerance is set to exact zero only when every finite source minute in the selected window is exactly zero; missing minutes remain missing Preserves the non-negative measurement domain without treating missing observations as zeros. Longest period No identifiability rule stated All-available value treated as an observed lower bound; an exactly identified period is a sensitivity Gaps cannot be mistaken for a continuously observed period. Participant correlations Correlation matrices requested Spearman coefficients and intervals are descriptive only, without a second significance screen The site-adjusted model family remains the inferential analysis. Current scientific deviations Placement roles and matched comparison: DEV-001 , REP-001 , and REP-002 . Site-adjusted H05 association models rather than pooled correlations: DEV-028 . Four factors × 17 metrics and complete 68-test FDR families: DEV-029 . Current window, timing, and continuous-period rules: DEV-054 . Current mean of viable one-minute MDER ratios: DEV-058 . Resolved implementation history Complete-vector FDR adjustment replaced the historical scalar adjustment: IMP-001 . Site-adjusted model inference replaced the historical inconsistent correlation display: IMP-006 . The two IMP entries are resolved history, not additional current methods or open qualifications.

text: Source data and technical provenance Exact source-data links accompany each result, model-check display, and sensitivity analysis above. The full data-preparation, model-construction, model-check, and output lineage is documented in the H05 analysis preparation and provenance . Implementation history for the current MDER and numerical-zero rules The current MDER outputs were produced by bounded MDER-only updates that preserved all non-MDER raw tests and fitted objects. The primary and gap-timing-unaware preservation records are the MDER reconciliation and gap MDER reconciliation . For darkest-10-hour mean melEDI, applying the current numerical-zero rule changed three primary near-eye and five primary chest participant-days from approximately 4.16 × 10 -17 lx to exactly 0 lx without changing a fitted sample. Only the corresponding primary models, model checks, influence checks, matched comparison, and mathematically dependent complete FDR families were updated. Coefficients changed by at most 3.61 × 10 -12 per LEBA point; two adjusted p -values changed below three-decimal display precision, no family rank changed, and all three families retained zero of 68 associations. The gap-timing-unaware L10 values were already exact zeros and were not refitted.

title: H05 analysis preparation and provenance – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: About this analysis record Note About this analysis record This page explains how verified light-exposure metrics and questionnaire scores were turned into the H05 results. Rendering it recalculates only file-identity, schema, and key checks plus lightweight descriptive summaries from the stored H05 model frames. It reads fitted models, estimates, intervals, model checks, influence screens, and predefined alternative analyses from their recorded files. It does not fit or refit a model, calculate predictions, repeat model checks, rerun leave-one-site-out analyses, bootstrap, or simulate data. H05 asks whether four Light Exposure Behaviour Assessment (LEBA) questionnaire factors are associated with 17 personal light-exposure metrics. The primary analysis uses the near-eye sensor position, which measures light close to the eyes. All-available chest measurements provide complementary evidence but are not interpreted as ocular exposure. A participant-day is one eligible local calendar day from one participant; participant-day metrics can therefore include repeated days from the same person. Factor effects are reported per one participant-level standard deviation (SD) of the score, with a 95% confidence interval (95% CI). Each inferential placement or dataset applies false-discovery-rate (FDR) adjustment to the complete family of four factors × 17 metrics = 68 tests. Participant-level and participant-day metrics use different model structures but share the same fixed-site adjustment, which estimates one adjustment coefficient for each study site, as well as the same questionnaire-score scaling and family definition. This page identifies the data and code that produced those results, explains why each analytical operation was necessary, and shows the stored evidence used to check the analysis. Read it alongside the H05 results report ; the exact H05 linked registration-record summary is mapped there once.

text: Factor construction The four LEBA factors are complete-score sums. Ordered item responses run from 1 (“Never”) to 5 (“Always”). The table identifies each behavioural factor and its construction rule before the factor codes are used alone. A factor score is non-estimable if any contributing item is missing. title: H05 analysis preparation and provenance – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Coverage, gaps, and metric support The primary dataset applied the general requirement of at least 50% valid minutes per hour and at least 80% valid hours per day, together with metric-specific support rules where the timing of remaining gaps affects what the metric can represent. Unsupported values remained missing rather than being interpreted as darkness. Light-level metrics use melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance (melEDI) in reader-facing labels, with a 0.1 lx offset where a logarithmic transform requires it. A Tweedie model is a positive-response regression model used here for non-negative, right-skewed durations while retaining exact zeros. A sensitivity analysis repeats the accepted comparison under a predefined alternative to assess whether the interpretation is stable. One predefined sensitivity uses the gap-timing-unaware dataset . It still passed the general 50%-per-hour and 80%-per-day coverage rules, but the timing of the remaining missing observations was not used for an additional metric-specific adjustment. For contrast at this first explanation, the primary dataset could be interpreted as a time-sensitive primary metric dataset . Hereafter it is called simply the primary dataset. MDER is the arithmetic mean of viable one-minute melEDI/illuminance ratios. Both channels must be finite and strictly positive, and at least 720 of the complete 1,440 local wall-clock minutes must provide a viable ratio. Repeated local minutes at daylight-saving fall-back are averaged channel-wise before forming the ratio; absent spring-forward minutes remain missing. Each viable minute ratio has equal weight: there is no time-profile weighting, gating, or scaling, and the daily value is not a ratio of daily integrals. Failure of this support rule makes only MDER missing; it does not delete the day from other metric analyses. The longest continuous period above 250 lx melEDI is an observed lower bound when a gap can interrupt the period. Its exact-identifiability sensitivity therefore retains only participant-days for which the longest period is fully observed. The L10 midpoint retains its continuous range and its strict-after-16:00 representation; no noon sensitivity was needed. The shared derivation rules are documented in Preparation 04 , and the model-ready datasets are documented in Preparation 06 . text: 3. Models, estimands, and inference

title: H05 analysis preparation and provenance – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
section: Estimand, practical effects, uncertainty, and multiplicity
text: Estimand, practical effects, uncertainty, and multiplicity For each metric and factor, the full model adds the centred LEBA score to the reduced site-adjusted model. A likelihood-ratio comparison asks whether the full model describes the data better than the reduced model on a common likelihood basis. The raw inferential p -value comes from that comparison. Each declared family contains all 17 metrics × 4 factors = 68 tests, and FDR adjustment is performed on the complete 68-value vector. Support is retained at adjusted p ≤ 0.050, decided before display formatting. Back-transformation converts a fitted-scale coefficient into the practical response scale used for interpretation. Coefficients are back-transformed and reported per one participant-level LEBA SD. Gaussian identity outcomes return a difference in the stated metric unit, log-transformed and Tweedie outcomes return a ratio, IS returns an odds ratio, and clock-time outcomes return a difference in hours. Every reported 95% CI is a two-sided Wald interval from the final model. No secondary significance screen is attached to descriptive sensitivities. Show the R code used for this display family_labels <- c ( ` H05-F1-primary ` = "Primary near eye" , ` H05-F2-complementary-chest ` = "Complementary chest" , ` H05-F3-manuscript-prepared ` = "Gap-timing-unaware near-eye sensitivity" ) family_audit |> transmute ( Family = unname (family_labels[.data $ family_id]), ` Planned tests ` = .data $ planned_tests, ` Observed tests ` = .data $ observed_tests, ` Adjusted tests ` = .data $ estimable_adjusted_tests, ` Retained at FDR 0.050 ` = .data $ passes_bh_0_05, ` Complete-vector check ` = if_else (.data $ vector_bh_verified, "Verified" , "Review needed" ) ) |> gt :: gt ( rowname_col = "Family" ) |> gt :: fmt_integer ( columns = where (is.numeric)) |> gt :: tab_source_note ( "Zero of 68 primary associations retained FDR-adjusted support. The same zero-retained result occurs in the complementary and gap-timing-unaware families." ) |> prep_gt () Table 8: Complete-family multiplicity audit for the three declared H05 inferential families. Planned tests Observed tests Adjusted tests Retained at FDR 0.050 Complete-vector check Primary near eye 68 68 68 0 Verified Complementary chest 68 68 68 0 Verified Gap-timing-unaware near-eye sensitivity 68 68 68 0 Verified Zero of 68 primary associations retained FDR-adjusted support. The same zero-retained result occurs in the complementary and gap-timing-unaware families. Note Why a less conservative adjustment can accompany fewer retained associations For one unchanged vector of raw p -values, the complete-vector FDR adjustment used here cannot retain fewer associations than Bonferroni at the same 0.050 threshold. The H05 family above is based on likelihood-ratio p -values from the fixed-site models. It is therefore not interchangeable with a family built from unadjusted rank correlations or another raw test. Multiplicity adjustment and the construction of the raw p -values are separate analytical decisions; the latter can change which associations enter the smallest ranks before either correction is applied.

title: H05 analysis preparation and provenance – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Site specification A fixed site effect gives each study site its own adjustment coefficient. A random site effect instead represents between-site variation through one estimated variance component. The fixed-site primary specification differs from the registered random-site structure. The decision was based on the inherited 17-metric site-structure evidence: every fixed-site model converged with a positive-definite Hessian and none was singular, whereas the random-site descriptions contained unstable, non-estimable, and singular fits. Keeping site fixed also estimates each site’s adjustment directly rather than relying on a variance component from only nine sites. This is an adjustment for observed site differences, not a claim that site causes an exposure outcome. The random-site structure remains a sensitivity. This is consistent with using fixed site for primary inference and random site only as a stability assessment.

section: Exact formulas supplied to the models
text: Exact formulas supplied to the models The analysis uses fixed site with sum-to-zero contrasts as the primary site adjustment. Participant-day models add a participant random effect because several days can come from the same participant. This random effect represents remaining between-participant variation after LEBA and site are considered. Participant-level IS and IV models contain one row per person and therefore do not add that effect. title: H05 analysis preparation and provenance – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Model-check sequence Every stored final model was checked for convergence, Hessian status, singularity, residual behaviour, response bounds, metric-specific timing support, and within-participant serial dependence where applicable. Gaussian models use transformed-residual and influence checks. Tweedie models add simulation-based uniformity, dispersion, zero-support, and outlier checks. Candidate influential participants were ranked by Cook’s distance for ordinary linear models or by maximum absolute Pearson residual for mixed models; this screen did not silently remove observations. The compact table below excludes the sleep-environment metric because that outcome has a separate, stronger disposition immediately afterwards. section: Numerical-zero normalization for darkest-10-hour mean melEDI
text: Numerical-zero normalization for darkest-10-hour mean melEDI The current rule sets a geometric-mean back-transformation residual to exact zero only when it lies within the unit-aware floating-point tolerance and every finite source minute entering the selected window is exactly zero. For these L10 windows, the tolerance is 2.220446049250313 × 10 -14 lx. Missing source minutes remain missing and are never imputed as zero. Under this rule, three primary near-eye and five primary chest participant-days are exact zero rather than approximately 4.163336342344337 × 10 -17 lx. This does not change a fitted sample, any non-L10 value, hourly or 30-minute value, participant-level value, or site/daylight-context value. The gap-timing-unaware L10 values were already exact zeros.

section: How to examine or reproduce H05
text: How to examine or reproduce H05 A reader can follow the analysis in five passes: inspect H05_input_audit.csv , h05_contract.R , and the factor, metric, formula, and run registries to verify the frozen inputs and specifications; compare the exact samples above with H05_model_frame_index.csv and the 136 frames in H05_model_frames.rds ; follow run_h05_stage2.R through h05_modeling.R , then the bounded MDER and L10 reseal scripts, to connect each frame to its current model object, coefficient, interval, likelihood-ratio test, diagnostic, and sensitivity record; inspect the complete 68-value family audit before interpreting any individual association; and read the H05 results report alongside its tables, figures, and paired source data. The most important boundary is that the preparation record documents a frozen analysis; it does not create an alternate result. If an input, metric rule, response model, or estimand changes, the affected scientific pipeline must be rerun before this page is refreshed.

title: H06: Day type, exercise, sleep, and personal light exposure – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: H06: Day type, exercise, sleep, and personal light exposure Associations with mean hourly melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance among observed hours that met support criteria Last modified: August 11, 2026
crumbs: H06 · Findings: day type, exercise, sleep

title: H06: Day type, exercise, sleep, and personal light exposure – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Scientific question The preregistered hypothesis was: H6: Day type, daily exercise, and sleep variables predict daily light exposure metrics. The main H06 analysis deliberately narrows that broad question to the zero-aware geometric mean of melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance (melEDI) in each observed one-hour interval that met the support criteria. It asks whether estimated mean hourly near-eye melEDI differs for free versus work days, active versus sedentary day status, and per one additional hour of previous sleep. It averages over retained hours rather than estimating daily light-exposure metrics. Time of day is examined separately and exploratorily. Near-eye measurements are primary; chest measurements provide complementary, non-ocular evidence. Neither position is a direct retinal measure. The complementary participant-day analysis , which treats one calendar day from one participant as the analytical unit, addresses daily light-exposure metrics. It is complementary evidence, while this hourly report remains the main H06 analysis. The two reports answer related but different questions, so their estimates are not interchangeable. How the hourly H06 analysis was prepared traces the inputs, fitted samples, formulas, model checks, sensitivity analyses, and source data underlying this report. Note Answer in brief Primary result. After false-discovery-rate adjustment, activity status ( FDR-adjusted p < 0.001 ) and day type ( FDR-adjusted p = 0.004 ) met the adjusted 0.050 threshold. Previous sleep did not (FDR-adjusted p = 0.745). Qualification. The day-type association is site- and model-dependent. Chest, paired-day, dataset-sensitivity, and model-check results provide complementary qualifications. The primary conclusions were also stable in a near-eye-only sensitivity that excluded six participants outside the employment requirement. Timing context. The nonlinear clock-time analysis is exploratory. Its intervals describe individual displayed times, not a simultaneous or multiplicity-controlled whole-curve test. All reported associations are observational.

title: H06: Day type, exercise, sleep, and personal light exposure – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Reader orientation A participant-hour is one observed one-hour interval from one participant that met the support criteria; a participant-day is one calendar day contributed by one participant. The analysis reports the estimated mean hourly melEDI among observed hours that met the support criteria. Because participant-days contribute different numbers of retained participant-hours, the main estimand gives more weight to days with more observed hours. Near-eye measurements are primary because the sensor position is closer to ocular light exposure. Chest measurements are complementary, non-ocular evidence. Neither sensor is a direct retinal measure. A participant-cluster-robust 95% confidence interval (95% CI) allows observations from the same participant to be related and uses the HC3 small-sample correction. False-discovery-rate adjustment is used for each declared set of related tests and is abbreviated FDR below. A predictor-by-site interaction model allows an association to differ by study site. Its site-average estimate is an average across sites that gives each site equal weight. A sensitivity analysis asks whether a conclusion changes when a defined feature of the dataset, sample, covariance correction, working variance, site weighting, calendar label, participant or site inclusion, or response model is changed.

title: H06: Day type, exercise, sleep, and personal light exposure – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Principal hourly result Figure 1 summarizes the common-effect estimates and their supporting sensor-position, paired-day, and dataset comparisons. Figure 1: Estimated mean hourly melEDI among observed hours that met the support criteria. Points and bars are ratios and participant-cluster-robust 95% CIs; the dashed line is the null ratio of 1. Near-eye is the primary sensor position, and chest estimates are complementary non-ocular comparisons. Source CSV Table 1 gives the three primary common-effect tests. Table 1: Primary near-eye associations. Predictor Ratio (95% CI) FDR-adjusted p Free day versus work day 1.45 × (1.14–1.85) 0.004 Active versus sedentary 2.06 × (1.54–2.76) <0.001 Previous sleep duration (per hour) 0.98 × (0.85–1.12) 0.745 Directions are free versus work day, active versus sedentary day status, and the ratio per one additional hour of previous sleep. Participant-cluster-robust 95% CIs use HC3 with 137 participants. The three p-values form one FDR-adjusted family; the null ratio is 1. Estimated mean hourly near-eye melEDI among observed hours that met the support criteria was 1.45 times as high on free as on work days (95% CI 1.14–1.85; FDR-adjusted p = 0.004) and 2.06 times as high on active as on sedentary days (1.54–2.76; FDR-adjusted p < 0.001). The ratio per one additional hour of previous sleep was 0.98 (0.85–1.12; FDR-adjusted p = 0.745). That interval allows a modest decrease or increase; it does not establish the absence of an association.

title: H06: Day type, exercise, sleep, and personal light exposure – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Site dependence The work/free association differed across study sites (FDR-adjusted p = 0.017). Activity and previous sleep had no FDR-retained predictor-by-site interaction. In the interaction model, the site-average work/free ratio, calculated with equal weight for each site, was 1.15 (95% CI 0.93–1.44), compared with 1.45 in the common-effect model. The interaction model’s site-average day-type association did not meet the adjusted threshold (three-predictor FDR-adjusted p = 0.298). Day type also did not meet the adjusted threshold when the working variance changed (FDR-adjusted p = 0.260). The day-type conclusion is therefore site- and model-dependent. Only adjusted p-values at alpha = 0.050 are bolded. The work/free association differed across sites (FDR-adjusted p = 0.017). Activity and previous sleep had no FDR-retained site interaction. The primary 1.45 work/free ratio comes from a model that constrains this association to be common across sites; it is not the average of the ratios from the interaction model. In the interaction model, the site-average ratio is the geometric mean of the nine site ratios: 1.15 (95% CI 0.93–1.44). Three sites are above that average and six are below it because three larger positive log-scale departures balance six smaller negative departures. This is not an algebraic inconsistency, but the attenuation from 1.45 to 1.15 shows that the work/free conclusion depends on model structure. The interaction-model site averages remain close to the common-effect results for activity (1.93 versus 2.06) and previous sleep (0.97 versus 0.98). text: Sensitivity and complementary sensor evidence The required gap-timing-unaware dataset uses the same 50%-per-hour and 80%-per-day coverage rules as the primary dataset, but does not use the timing of the remaining within-hour and within-day gaps for a metric-specific adjustment. The primary analysis could therefore be interpreted as time-sensitive. The near-eye estimates were stable under this dataset change, including on exact common hours. Complementary chest estimates had similar directions. The paired-day comparison used the same 109 participants and 553 participant-days at both sensor positions, but three hourly keys differed at each position. It is not an observation-level identity comparison, an equivalence analysis, or a direct sensor-position effect. Activity and previous-sleep conclusions were stable across the declared checks. Day type remained sensitive to the working variance and to omission of some sites. A separate near-eye-only sensitivity excluded participants recorded as not employed or marginally employed. It retained all nine sites and classified all three primary associations as stable within model uncertainty. Show complementary placement and sensitivity results

text: Nonlinear time-of-day GAM analysis The exploratory nonlinear generalized additive model (GAM) analysis allows the associations with local clock time to bend across the day. It separates occurrence (melEDI greater than zero, binomial-logit) from positive magnitude (Gamma-log); multiplying their response-scale means gives estimated hourly melEDI. Both components use four cyclic factor-by clock smooths for work/free day × activity status, with one smoothing parameter shared across the four curves. Study site enters as a fixed adjustment only; there is no site-specific clock smooth and no sz component. Participant and participant-day random-effect smooths, true-sequence AR.start , and residual working correlations remain. title: H06: Day type, exercise, sleep, and personal light exposure – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Interpretation and limitations The common-effect results describe observational associations with estimated mean hourly near-eye melEDI among observed hours that met the support criteria. They do not establish causal effects and do not answer the broader preregistered question about daily light-exposure metrics. Participant-days with more retained participant-hours contribute more weight. The free/work result is qualified by its predictor-by-site interaction, the smaller site-average estimate from that interaction model, the alternative working-variance result, and leave-one-site-out checks. Chest and paired-day analyses provide complementary non-ocular context, not sensor-position equivalence or a direct placement effect. Participant-cluster-robust inference allows within-participant dependence, but it does not remove residual time-of-day structure or repair an imperfect mean model. The nonlinear GAM analysis is exploratory; its pointwise intervals apply to individual displayed hours and do not support simultaneous whole-curve claims.

section: Outcome, predictors, sensor positions, and fitted samples
text: Outcome, predictors, sensor positions, and fitted samples The primary outcome is the zero-aware geometric mean melEDI for each retained participant-hour at the near-eye sensor position. A participant-hour is one observed one-hour interval from one participant that met the support criteria defined in Preparation 06 . Activity is binary: sedentary means no reported exercise, while active includes light, moderate, or vigorous reported exercise. Day type and activity are participant-day diary variables, where a participant-day is one calendar day contributed by one participant; previous sleep duration is linked from the preceding sleep period. Because participant-days contribute 19–24 supported participant-hours, the estimand is participant-hour weighted rather than participant-day weighted. The KNUST_S005 numeral 3,600 is interpreted as 3,600 seconds, or one sedentary hour, only for eligible exploratory analyses; it is not added to the primary analysis. For the required sensitivity analysis, the gap-timing-unaware dataset applies the same 50%-per-hour and 80%-per-day coverage rules but does not use the timing of remaining missing observations for a metric-specific adjustment. text: Models and inference The common-effect model is a zero-inclusive quasi-Poisson generalized linear model with a log link and fixed study-site terms. A participant-cluster-robust 95% confidence interval (95% CI) allows observations from the same participant to be related and uses the HC3 small-sample correction. Participants, rather than participant-hours, are therefore the inferential replicates. One-coefficient tests use a t reference with 136 degrees of freedom. The predictor-by-site interaction model allows the association of day type, activity, or previous sleep with hourly melEDI to differ by study site. Its site-interaction blocks use Wald F tests with restriction-rank and 136 denominator degrees of freedom. title: H06 analysis preparation and provenance – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: H06 analysis preparation and provenance Show All Code Hide All Code View Source From supported one-hour personal-light records and linked diaries to day-type, activity, and previous-sleep contrasts Last modified: August 14, 2026 This page records how the hourly H06 analysis was prepared. It follows melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance (melEDI) from observed hours that met the support criteria through the reported models and displays. A participant-hour is one observed one-hour interval from one participant that met the support criteria; a participant-day is one calendar day contributed by one participant. The near-eye sensor position is primary because it is closer to ocular light exposure. The chest sensor position is complementary and represents non-ocular exposure. The Hourly H06 results report gives the associations, uncertainty, model checks, and interpretation. The complementary participant-day report addresses daily light-exposure metrics. The hourly analysis remains the main H06 analysis, and the two estimands are not interchangeable. Note About this analysis record This page reads the reviewed stored frames, tables, model-check outputs, figures, and file identities for display. It does not repeat model fitting or scientific computation. In particular, it does not fit or refit a model, generate model predictions, estimate residual correlation, rerun a sensitivity analysis, resample, or simulate.

section: Day type, activity, and previous sleep
text: Day type, activity, and previous sleep work_free_day is a participant-day diary label: Work day or Free day. activity_status is Sedentary when no exercise was reported and Active when light, moderate, or vigorous exercise was reported. The four original intensity labels are not used as separate primary levels. previous_sleep_duration_h is taken from the preceding eligible sleep period and centred at 8 h. The fitted coefficient is therefore the ratio for one additional hour of previous sleep. Show the R code used for this display previous_night_linkage |> transmute ( ` Onset relative to wake date ` = recode ( .data $ onset_to_wake_date_relation, onset_on_wake_date_after_midnight = "After midnight on the wake date" , onset_on_preceding_date = "On the preceding date" , unavailable = "Unavailable" ), ` Diary rows ` = .data $ diary_rows, Quarantined = .data $ quarantined_rows, ` Eligible for analysis ` = .data $ analysis_eligible_rows ) |> gt :: gt () |> gt :: fmt_integer ( columns = where (is.numeric)) |> h06_gt () Table 7: Previous-night temporal linkage audit Onset relative to wake date Diary rows Quarantined Eligible for analysis After midnight on the wake date 650 0 650 On the preceding date 625 0 625 Unavailable 1 1 0 The sleep onset may lie on the preceding calendar date or after midnight on the wake date. Both relations are valid when they belong to the same eligible sleep interval; the one unavailable interval is quarantined. This prevents a calendar-date join from assigning sleep to the wrong participant-day.

text: Primary model and estimands

title: H06 analysis preparation and provenance – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Exact formulas The quasi-Poisson model estimates a log mean while allowing the response variance to differ from a Poisson variance. Study site enters as a fixed effect, so the model adjusts for the listed sites rather than treating them as a random sample of sites. A participant-cluster-robust 95% CI allows hours from the same participant to be related and uses the HC3 small-sample correction. The predictor-by-site interaction model allows an association to differ by study site. A site-average estimate gives each included site equal weight on the log scale, then back-transforms once to the reported ratio. Show the R code used for this display primary_formula_registry |> gt :: gt () |> gt :: cols_label ( model = "Model" , wilkinson_formula = "Wilkinson formula" , purpose = "Purpose" ) |> gt :: fmt_markdown ( columns = "wilkinson_formula" ) |> gt :: tab_style ( style = gt :: cell_text ( font = gt :: google_font ( "Roboto Mono" ), size = gt :: px ( 11 )), locations = gt :: cells_body ( columns = "wilkinson_formula" ) ) |> h06_gt ( font_size = 11 ) Table 15: Exact Wilkinson formulas used for the common-effect and predictor-by-site interaction models Model Wilkinson formula Purpose Primary additive model response_value ~ site + work_free_day + activity_status + previous_sleep_duration_centered_h Average association for each of the three prespecified predictors Predictor-by-site interaction model response_value ~ site * work_free_day + site * activity_status + site * previous_sleep_duration_centered_h Site-specific associations and three omnibus site-interaction tests The common-effect formula asks whether estimated mean hourly near-eye melEDI among observed hours that met the support criteria differs for free versus work days, active versus sedentary day status, and per one additional hour of previous sleep. The null ratio is 1. Local clock time is not a primary predictor. The predictor-by-site interaction formula allows each of those three associations to differ by study site; it is not a different reference outcome or a test of whether a site lies above the site-average association, which gives each included site equal weight. The quasi-Poisson specification is used as a log-mean estimating model, not as a claim that the observed melEDI distribution is Poisson. A participant-cluster-robust 95% confidence interval (95% CI) allows observations from the same participant to be related and uses the HC3 small-sample correction. The site-average estimate gives each included site equal weight and then back-transforms once; participant-hours do not determine site weights. Show the R code used for this display model_settings |> gt :: gt () |> gt :: cols_label ( setting = "Setting" , implementation = "Specification" , interpretation = "What it fixes" ) |> h06_gt ( font_size = 11 ) Table 16: Primary model, covariance, and contrast settings Setting Specification What it fixes Mean and link Quasi-Poisson mean with log link; working variance power 1 Estimated zero-aware geometric-mean melEDI for an observed hour that met support criteria Site adjustment Fixed site effects with sum contrasts The site-average ratios give each included site equal weight Repeated observations Participant-cluster HC3 covariance with finite-cluster correction Hours may repeat within participant-days and participants Reference coding Work day; Sedentary; previous sleep centred at 8 h Ratios compare Free versus Work, Active versus Sedentary, and one additional hour of sleep Uncertainty 95% confidence intervals with participants minus one degrees of freedom Finite-participant rather than asymptotic normal inference Back-transformation Standardized log means are exponentiated once Reported contrasts are ratios of estimated mean hourly melEDI

title: H06 analysis preparation and provenance – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: False-discovery-rate adjustment False-discovery-rate (FDR) adjustment is applied within each declared family of related tests below. Show the R code used for this display multiplicity_registry |> arrange (.data $ family_order) |> transmute ( Family = .data $ content, Tests = .data $ planned_size, Adjustment = "FDR" ) |> gt :: gt () |> gt :: fmt_integer ( columns = "Tests" ) |> h06_gt () Table 17: Declared false-discovery-rate adjustment families Family Tests Adjustment Primary near-eye main-association tests 3 FDR Primary near-eye site-heterogeneity tests 3 FDR Primary equal-site practical contrasts 3 FDR Gap-timing-unaware near-eye main tests 3 FDR Gap-timing-unaware near-eye heterogeneity tests 3 FDR The three primary common-effect tests, three primary site-interaction tests, and three practical standardized contrasts form separate FDR families. The near-eye gap-timing-unaware counterparts use separate three-test families. Only FDR-adjusted p-values are interpreted in the results report. The exploratory site-specific display applies a separate nine-site FDR adjustment within each predictor rather than pooling all 27 site estimates. Those site-wise tests compare each site’s ratio with the null ratio 1; they do not test whether sites differ from the site-average association or from one another.

title: H06 analysis preparation and provenance – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Preregistration decisions DEV-015 records the documented hourly geometric-mean melEDI estimand rather than the preregistered daily metric set. DEV-030 limits the primary family to day type, active/sedentary status, and previous-night sleep duration. DEV-031 records the zero-inclusive quasi-Poisson common-effect model, participant-cluster HC3 inference, predictor-by-site interactions, and separate exploratory nonlinear clock-time analysis. DEV-032 records the separate FDR families and the distinction between average associations, predictor-by-site interactions, and exploratory site screens. These choices are summarized with the results under Linked registration-record summary .

title: H06 analysis preparation and provenance – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Nonlinear local-clock GAM analysis Time of day is described separately from the three primary average associations. This nonlinear generalized additive model (GAM) analysis allows the associations with local clock time to bend across the day. It has two parts: a binomial model for whether hourly melEDI is positive and a Gamma log-link model for the positive magnitude. Their response-scale product gives estimated mean hourly melEDI. Show the R code used for this display temporal_formula_registry |> filter (.data $ selected_basis_k == 16 L) |> transmute ( Component = recode ( .data $ component, occurrence = "Occurrence" , positive_magnitude = "Positive magnitude" ), Family = .data $ response_family, Formula = gsub ( "[[:space:]]+" , " " , .data $ selected_formula), Method = .data $ method, ` Discrete computation ` = dplyr :: if_else ( .data $ discrete, "Yes" , "No" ), ` Basis k ` = .data $ selected_basis_k, ` Site-specific clock smooth ` = dplyr :: if_else ( .data $ site_specific_clock_smooth, "Yes" , "No" ), Role = "Exploratory clock-time context" ) |> gt :: gt () |> gt :: fmt_markdown ( columns = "Formula" ) |> gt :: tab_style ( style = gt :: cell_text ( font = gt :: google_font ( "Roboto Mono" ), size = gt :: px ( 10.5 )), locations = gt :: cells_body ( columns = "Formula" ) ) |> h06_gt ( font_size = 10.5 ) Table 23: Exact formulas for the exploratory two-part clock-time model Component Family Formula Method Discrete computation Basis k Site-specific clock smooth Role Occurrence Binomial occurrence with logit link melEDI_positive ~ previous_sleep_duration_centered_h + site + work_free_day * activity_status + s(clock_hour, by = day_activity_group, bs = “cc”, k = 16, id = 1) + s(participant_key, bs = “re”) + s(participant_day_key, bs = “re”) fREML Yes 16 No Exploratory clock-time context Positive magnitude Gamma positive magnitude with log link response_value ~ previous_sleep_duration_centered_h + site + work_free_day * activity_status + s(clock_hour, by = day_activity_group, bs = “cc”, k = 16, id = 1) + s(participant_key, bs = “re”) + s(participant_day_key, bs = “re”) fREML Yes 16 No Exploratory clock-time context The four day-type-by-activity curves use cyclic cubic factor-by smooths with a shared smoothing parameter. They are not sum-to-zero site-deviation smooths, and no site-specific clock smooth is fitted. Site enters parametrically, and the displayed curves average equally across the nine near-eye sites. Both components use fREML and discrete = TRUE ; no discrete = FALSE computation is required. Show the R code used for this display temporal_fit_summary |> filter (.data $ selected_for_exploratory_display) |> transmute ( Component = recode ( .data $ component, occurrence = "Occurrence" , positive_magnitude = "Positive magnitude" ), Observations = .data $ observations, ` Participant-days ` = .data $ participant_days, Participants = .data $ participants, Sequences = .data $ analysis_sequences, ` Basis k ` = .data $ basis_k, ` Working rho ` = .data $ working_ar_rho, Converged = dplyr :: if_else (.data $ converged, "Yes" , "No" ), ` Deviance explained ` = .data $ deviance_explained ) |> gt :: gt () |> gt :: fmt_integer ( columns = c ( "Observations" , "Participant-days" , "Participants" , "Sequences" , "Basis k" )) |> gt :: fmt_number ( columns = "Working rho" , decimals = 3 ) |> gt :: fmt_percent ( columns = "Deviance explained" , decimals = 1 ) |> h06_gt ( font_size = 11 ) Table 24: Stored model checks for the selected exploratory clock-time components Component Observations Participant-days Participants Sequences Basis k Working rho Converged Deviance explained Occurrence 16,596 715 137 1,052 16 0.418 Yes 63.2% Positive magnitude 11,899 715 137 1,370 16 0.440 Yes 45.2% The selected occurrence component uses all 16,596 primary hours; the positive magnitude component uses 11,899 positive hours. Removing zeros splits some positive-magnitude sequences, so residual correlation never bridges an excluded zero. The working residual correlations are approximately 0.418 and 0.440. The AR(1) working structure relates residuals in adjacent supported hours within a true-time sequence, with the working relation weakening across larger lags. It is a GEE-like working adjustment for these non-Gaussian bam fits, not a fully generative joint autoregressive likelihood. title: H06 daily metrics: day-level context and personal light exposure – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Scientific question The signed hypothesis states: “Day type (weekday/weekend; free/work day), daily exercise, and sleep variables predict daily light exposure metrics.” This complementary analysis asks that question with one row per admissible metric-specific participant-day. It does not give days with more supported hours greater weight. The completed hourly H06 analysis is the selected main H06 result. This participant-day analysis is complementary, preregistration-oriented evidence. The two analyses are related but have different outcomes and weighting; neither result substitutes for the other. The analysis-preparation and provenance companion documents the exact inputs, models, checks, and stored outputs used here. Note Answer in brief In the primary near-eye analysis, false-discovery-rate (FDR) adjustment, which limits the expected proportion of false discoveries within each prespecified 15-slot family, retained associations for 10 of 14 estimable metrics with Free versus Work day, 6 of 14 with Active versus Sedentary status, and 12 of 14 per additional hour of previous-night sleep. Every retained association requires the model-check qualifications (model diagnostics), which assess fit, support, residual behavior, and sensitivity evidence, described below. For outcomes fitted as \log_{10}(Y + 0.1) , Y remains in its stated unit, such as lx for melEDI, h for continuous periods, or lx h for dose. The back-transformed ratios compare fitted geometric-mean-like values of Y + 0.1 ; they are not ratios of raw metric means. Free days had lower fitted mean melEDI, M10 mean, waking time above 250 lx melEDI, longest continuous period above 250 lx melEDI, and melEDI dose than Work days. M10 and L10 midpoints and first light above 250 lx melEDI were later, whereas last light above 250 lx melEDI was earlier. Active days had higher fitted mean melEDI, M10 mean, time above 1,000 and 250 lx melEDI, longest continuous period above 250 lx melEDI, and melEDI dose than Sedentary days. Longer previous-night sleep was associated with lower fitted light-level, bright-duration, longest-period, and dose metrics; more time below 1 lx melEDI during sleep; and later M10, L10, mean-light, and first-light timing. Ten primary predictor-by-site interaction blocks, which allow an association to differ among sites, met their separate 15-slot FDR rule. For example, the interaction model estimated lower Free-day mean melEDI at every site, with pointwise 95% confidence intervals (95% CIs) excluding 1 at Dortmund (DE), Tübingen (DE), Madrid (ES), and Kumasi (GH). A pointwise interval assesses one site estimate at a time and is not a simultaneous band. The global interaction test establishes variation across sites, while the site intervals describe where the fitted site-specific contrasts are clearest. In the exploratory mutually adjusted daily models, activity estimates were stable after adding day type and sleep. Three sleep estimates and four work/free estimates shifted by 1 to less than 2 standard errors. One work/free estimate, time below 1 lx melEDI during sleep, reversed direction and shifted by more than 3 standard errors. Mean melEDI nevertheless remained lower on Free days after adjustment, with a fitted ratio of 0.75 (95% CI 0.68 to 0.82; FDR q < 0.001). The separate nonlinear generalized additive mixed model (GAMM) analysis of 30-minute bins allowed context associations to vary smoothly over clock time while accounting for repeated measurements. It found time-varying profiles for day type, activity, within-participant sleep, and between-participant sleep in its four-test exploratory FDR family. The selected main hourly H06 analysis does not give the same answer as the daily mean metric: hourly melEDI was higher on Free days, whereas the participant-day mean metric was lower. This difference is scientifically plausible because the analyses use different outcomes, weighting, and model structures. The overall two-part L10 mean result remains non-estimable, and all three primary MDER 95% intervals included zero. The gap-timing-unaware analysis is reported only as a sensitivity.

title: H06 daily metrics: day-level context and personal light exposure – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Outcomes, contexts, and sample roles The 15 participant-day outcomes comprise mean melEDI; M10 and L10 mean melEDI; four threshold-duration measures; the longest continuous period above 250 lx melEDI; M10 and L10 midpoint; mean, first, and last timing above 250 lx melEDI; melEDI dose; and melanopic daylight efficacy ratio (MDER). “Period” describes the continuous-duration metric. Sleep-period light is interpreted as the bedside sleep environment, not verified ocular exposure. The three primary contexts were: Free versus Work day; Active versus Sedentary daily activity status; and each additional hour of previous-night sleep duration, centered at 8 h. Near-eye measurements are primary. All-available chest results are a complementary non-ocular comparison. Paired/common results compare the two placements after retaining the same participant-days in both placements. More generally, a common sample means that the compared models or placements use the same participant-days. The gap-timing-unaware dataset repeats the near-eye analysis as a separate metric-construction sensitivity. Table 1: Analysis roles and exact fitted-sample ranges. The nine study sites, in display order, are Borås (SE), Delft (NL), Dortmund (DE), Tübingen (DE), Munich (DE), Madrid (ES), Izmir (TR), San José (CR), Kumasi (GH). title: H06 daily metrics: day-level context and personal light exposure – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Models, contrasts, and multiplicity The non-timing outcomes use fixed study-site terms and a participant random intercept, which allows participants to have different baseline outcome levels. The primary models were fitted separately for each predictor, so their estimates are not mutually adjusted for the other two day-level contexts. The common-association and predictor-by-site interaction formulas are: response ~ site + predictor + (1 | participant) response ~ site * predictor + (1 | participant) Four clock outcomes, M10 midpoint, L10 midpoint, first timing above 250 lx melEDI, and last timing above 250 lx melEDI, use the corresponding fixed-site linear models with participant-cluster HC3 uncertainty. All displayed intervals are pointwise 95% confidence intervals (95% CIs) ; each assesses one estimate at a time, and none is simultaneous. A site-average estimate gives each included site equal weight, irrespective of its observed sample size. Multiplicity comprises 12 separate FDR families: primary and gap-timing-unaware datasets × three predictors × association or predictor-by-site interaction. Every family retains all 15 named metric slots. L10 mean remains the non-estimable slot 3 with missing raw and adjusted p-values; MDER occupies slot 15 and has no association FDR support. Table 2: Twelve fixed 15-slot FDR families. Claim-eligible counts additionally exclude MDER and retain all stated model-check limitations. Note How to read the estimates A site-average estimate gives every included site equal weight. It is not weighted by the number of observations contributed by each site. A predictor-by-site interaction allows the association between a context and an outcome to differ among sites. A global interaction test does not by itself identify which site estimates differ. A pointwise 95% CI describes uncertainty for one displayed estimate. It is not a simultaneous interval across sites, metrics, or clock times. An FDR adjustment limits the expected proportion of false discoveries among the tests in its explicitly defined family. A participant random intercept allows participants to have different baseline outcome levels. A common sample retains the same participant-days across the compared models or placements. Model checks cover fit, support, residual behavior, and sensitivity evidence. A working first-order autoregressive correlation, AR(1) , allows adjacent residuals within a participant-day sequence to be correlated.

title: H06 daily metrics: day-level context and personal light exposure – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Exploratory mutually adjusted daily analysis This exploratory batch directly addresses whether day type, activity, and previous-night sleep remain stable when included together. For each metric, one common complete-case near-eye frame was used for both the separate predictor models and the mutually adjusted model. For the 14 estimable metrics, this common sample contains 715 participant-days from 137 participants. Using the same rows prevents a sample change from being mistaken for covariate adjustment. For non-timing outcomes, the mutually adjusted formula was: response ~ site + day type + activity + previous-night sleep + (1 | participant) The predictor-by-site interaction models added one site × context block at a time while holding the other two contexts additive. This is the prespecified lower-dimensional implementation of the proposed site * day type + site * activity + site * sleep duration structure. It preserves all three main context terms but evaluates each interaction block without conditioning it on two other high-dimensional interaction blocks. The four timing outcomes used the corresponding fixed-site linear models with participant-cluster HC3 covariance. L10 mean remained the named non-estimable slot 3 and was not replaced. text: Exploratory 30-minute time-of-day GAMM This separate analysis asks how the shape of the 24-hour profile varies by day type, activity, and sleep. It is not a daily-metric sensitivity. The response is the 30-minute arithmetic mean melEDI, Y , transformed as \log_{10}(Y + 0.1\ \mathrm{lx}) . Its 33,057 supported half-hour bins come from 715 participant-days, 137 participants, and all nine sites. The accepted mgcv::bam() model used Gaussian identity errors, fREML, discrete = TRUE , one thread, and a frame-specific working AR(1) coefficient. This working correlation allows adjacent residuals within each audited participant-day sequence to be correlated. Its exact smooth structure was: s(time, bs = "cc", k = 12) + s(time, day type, bs = "sz", k = 12) + s(time, activity, bs = "sz", k = 12) + s(time, by = between-participant sleep, k = 12) + s(time, by = within-participant sleep, k = 12) + s(time, site, bs = "sz", k = 12) + s(time, participant, bs = "fs", k = 10) + s(participant-day, bs = "re") Only the global time smooth used the cyclic cubic basis. The sz , fs , and sleep time margins retained mgcv’s default thin-plate basis, with no cyclic xt request. Sleep was separated into the participant mean and the day’s deviation from that mean. Figure 5: Time-varying near-eye context associations from the exploratory 30-minute GAMM. Curves are ratios for fitted Y plus 0.1 lx; bands are pointwise 95% confidence intervals.
