The q-values are approximate whole-function tests in one four-test FDR family. All displayed curve intervals are pointwise, not simultaneous. All four whole-function tests met the exploratory FDR rule. The Free/Work ratio was lowest at 08:45, 0.20, but exceeded 1 after midnight, reaching 1.84. The Active/Sedentary ratio reached 1.62 at 15:15. One additional hour of sleep within participant was most strongly associated at 00:15, ratio 0.76. One additional hour of participant-mean sleep had its strongest fitted association at 08:45, ratio 0.61. These are time-varying observational associations on the shifted-response scale, not causal effects or raw melEDI ratios.

section: Comparison with the selected main H06 analysis
text: Comparison with the selected main H06 analysis The selected main H06 analysis and this complementary analysis do not estimate the same quantity. Main H06 gives each supported participant-hour one row and models the zero-aware geometric mean melEDI for that hour, with all three contexts in one model. H06_daily gives each admissible participant-day one row per metric. Its primary models are predictor-specific, while the exploratory joint column below uses a common 715-day frame and includes all three contexts. Where a global predictor-by-site interaction met its FDR rule, the table uses the site-average full contrast from that interaction model , with every site weighted equally, and gives the range of its nine full site-specific ratios. Otherwise it uses the additive model’s common contrast. The additive-family association q-value remains the prespecified association test, while the global interaction q-value determines which effect model is displayed. Table 13: Selected main hourly H06 versus daily mean-melEDI associations. Supported interaction rows use the site-average geometric mean of the nine full site-specific ratios from that model and show the site range. Other rows use the additive common contrast. Interaction-model site ratios are full contrasts and require no multiplication by a main effect. Numerical equality is neither expected nor claimed. The clearest contrast is day type, for which all three global site interactions were supported. The interaction-model site-average ratio was 1.15 (95% CI 0.93 to 1.44) in main hourly H06, with full site-specific ratios from 0.53 to 2.44. Daily mean melEDI was lower on Free days in both the predictor-specific interaction model, site-average ratio 0.70 (0.63 to 0.78; site range 0.40 to 0.95), and the mutually adjusted interaction model, 0.73 (0.66 to 0.81; site range 0.44 to 1.00). This is not a failed replication. The hourly analysis weights days by their supported hours and targets a retained hour’s geometric mean; the daily analysis weights admissible days equally and targets a daily metric. Activity was positive in all three analyses. Its primary daily interaction was supported, so that column uses the interaction-model site-average ratio 1.22 (1.08 to 1.39; full site ratios 0.84 to 2.26). The main hourly and mutually adjusted daily activity interactions were not supported, so their displayed 2.06 and 1.16 ratios come from additive models. Previous sleep had no supported site interaction in any column. It was compatible with little hourly association, additive ratio 0.98 and FDR q = 0.745, but was associated with lower daily mean melEDI, additive ratios 0.89 and 0.90. The analyses therefore provide related but non-interchangeable evidence about hourly exposure and participant-day metrics.

title: H06 daily metrics: day-level context and personal light exposure – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Primary and gap-sensitivity daily grid All 468 non-L10 model cells passed the hard construct, support, numerical, and estimability gates, but every cell was classified acceptable with limitations after direct visual review of residual centering, variance, and gross distributional shape. No gross residual failure was observed. Temporal dependence was retained as a mandatory model-check sidecar rather than an automatic failure criterion. Actual-date AR counterparts were sometimes singular, numerically unresolved, or left residual dependence; those findings remain part of interpretation but do not replace the primary estimates or p-values. In the primary timing route, the first-light Work/Free Student-t estimate shifted by 1.23 participant-cluster HC3 standard errors, and the L10 midpoint activity AR estimate shifted by 1.26 HC3 standard errors. Timing predictor-by-site results remain sensitivity-dependent. Participant/site deletion checks were stable for 270 of 468 cells, showed a substantial limitation for 128, were unstable for 46, and had a non-estimable deletion refit for 24. Gaussian, Tweedie, Student-t, exact-period, and AR model-check sidecars are reported as response-family or stability limitations; none was used to substitute a p-value. text: Exploratory mutually adjusted daily models All 14 estimable joint models and their required additive and one-interaction structures were numerically estimable. Direct residual-plot review classified all 14 as review limitations and none as a gross failure. First-light timing retained a U-shaped residual pattern and heavy tails under the participant-HC3 route. MDER retained pronounced upper-tail and site-influence limitations. Actual-date residual lag was reported descriptively and did not replace or invalidate an otherwise usable model. No deletion batch, bootstrap, or simulation was added to this exploratory analysis.

title: H06 daily metrics: day-level context and personal light exposure – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Exploratory temporal GAMM Five of six fitted frames met the accepted formula, convergence, basis, residual, temporal-dependence, fixed-term-identifiability, and cyclic-closure rules. All six BAM fits converged without fitting warnings, but the paired chest frame did not meet the residual-scale extraction rule and contributed no association summary. In the primary near-eye fit, the residual Q-Q correlation was 0.965, the absolute-residual/fitted Spearman correlation was 0.293, final pooled lag-1 correlation was 0.090, and the largest absolute site lag-1 correlation was 0.159. The bounded k = 16 check supported retaining k = 12 . Participant and site deletion robustness remains untested for the GAMM, so its results stay exploratory. These are observational associations with recorded day-level contexts. They do not establish causal effects, health outcomes, identical associations across sites, or equivalence between sensor placements.

text: H06 daily-metric analysis preparation and provenance From participant-day light-exposure metrics and recorded contexts to complementary association estimates Last modified: August 13, 2026 This page explains how the complementary H06 participant-day analysis was prepared, fitted, checked, and translated into the reported tables and figures. The selected hourly H06 analysis remains the main H06 result. A participant-day is one eligible local calendar day from one participant. Each admissible light-exposure metric contributes at most one row for that participant-day, so days are not weighted by their number of supported hours. The complementary H06 daily-metric results report contains the association estimates, confidence intervals, multiplicity decisions, site-specific patterns, complementary analyses, and the comparison with the selected main hourly H06 analysis. Note Execution boundary This page verifies stored file identities and schemas and calculates only bounded descriptive summaries of the already fitted samples. Model estimates, predictions, residual correlation, p-values, false-discovery-rate (FDR) adjustments, deletion analyses, and nonlinear clock-time functions are read from stored outputs. FDR adjustment limits the expected proportion of false discoveries within each defined family. Rendering this page does not fit or refit a model, regenerate a prediction, rerun a sensitivity analysis, resample, or simulate.

text: Analysis path The primary path estimates each context separately for each daily metric. The predictor-by-site interaction path allows that association to differ among sites. Two exploratory paths then examine covariate stability and 30-minute clock-time profiles without changing the primary participant-day estimand. The nonlinear generalized additive mixed model (GAMM) analysis represents smooth clock-time variation while accounting for repeated measurements. Its working first-order autoregressive correlation, AR(1), allows adjacent residuals within a participant-day sequence to be correlated. A pointwise 95% confidence interval (95% CI) assesses one displayed estimate and is not a simultaneous band. Model checks assess fit, observed support, residual behavior, and sensitivity evidence. The back-transformed quantity is geometric-mean-like for Y + 0.1 in that unit; it is not the raw arithmetic mean of Y . The main response treatments were: \log_{10}(Y + 0.1) for zero-containing right-skewed level, continuous- period, and dose outcomes selected for the shifted-log Gaussian route; a Tweedie distribution with log link for non-negative duration outcomes with a point mass at zero and a continuous positive part; identity-scale Gaussian models for outcomes whose residual behavior was judged adequate on that scale; and clock hours for timing outcomes. L10 midpoint was unwrapped at 16:00 so that values after 16:00 and before the following morning occupy one continuous night-centred axis. Exact zero handling was metric-specific. Exact zeros remained in every one-part model whose response allowed zero. For the darkest 10 h mean, exact zeros remained in the occurrence component and were excluded only from the strictly positive magnitude component. Its joint two-part association was not estimable because the occurrence component separated, so its named multiplicity slot remains missing. Daily melanopic daylight efficacy ratio (MDER) is the arithmetic mean of viable positive finite one-minute melEDI/illuminance ratios. It requires at least 720 viable ratios on a complete 1,440-minute local wall-clock grid and is not a ratio of daily integrals.

text: Predictor-specific model hierarchy For each metric and predictor, the reduced model contains site and the repeated- participant structure. The additive model adds the predictor and estimates the site-average common association, giving each site equal weight. The interaction model adds the complete predictor-by-site block and tests whether the association varies among sites. Work day and Sedentary are the categorical references. All reported intervals are pointwise 95% CIs, not simultaneous intervals. Show the R code used for this display model_routes |> distinct ( .data $ reader_route, .data $ reduced_formula, .data $ additive_formula, .data $ heterogeneity_formula, .data $ uncertainty ) |> transmute ( Route = .data $ reader_route, Reduced = paste0 ( "`" , .data $ reduced_formula, "`" ), Additive = paste0 ( "`" , .data $ additive_formula, "`" ), ` Predictor-by-site interaction ` = paste0 ( "`" , .data $ heterogeneity_formula, "`" ), Uncertainty = .data $ uncertainty ) |> gt :: gt () |> gt :: fmt_markdown ( columns = c ( "Reduced" , "Additive" , "Predictor-by-site interaction" )) |> compact_gt ( font_size = 10 ) Table 9: Selected model routes and exact formula hierarchy Route Reduced Additive Predictor-by-site interaction Uncertainty Fixed-site mixed model with participant random intercept response_value ~ site + (1 | participant_key) response_value ~ site + predictor + (1 | participant_key) response_value ~ site * predictor + (1 | participant_key) Model-based pointwise 95% CI Two-part occurrence and positive magnitude route; joint slot not estimable response_value ~ site + (1 | participant_key) response_value ~ site + predictor + (1 | participant_key) response_value ~ site * predictor + (1 | participant_key) Component-specific intervals only; joint association and heterogeneity tests are non-estimable Fixed-site linear model with participant-cluster HC3 covariance response_value ~ site response_value ~ site + predictor response_value ~ site * predictor Participant-cluster HC3 covariance; participant clusters minus one degrees of freedom; pointwise 95% CI The four timing outcomes repaired to participant-cluster HC3 inference are M10 midpoint, L10 midpoint, first timing above 250 lx melEDI, and last timing above 250 lx melEDI. Their fixed-site linear models use participant-cluster HC3 covariance with finite-cluster adjustment and participant-clusters-minus-one degrees of freedom. Other estimable daily outcomes use their selected Gaussian or Tweedie mixed model with a participant random intercept, which allows participants to have different baseline outcome levels. The exact registered benchmark was retained without silent substitution: response_value ~ predictor + (predictor | site) + ( 1 | site : participant_key) It is a benchmark because nine sites provide limited support for a random site intercept, random predictor slope, and their correlation. The fixed-site route is the reported estimand. For categorical predictors it is the Free/Work or Active/Sedentary site-average contrast, with every site weighted equally. For previous sleep it is the association per additional hour, also averaged equally over sites. The interaction route reports the complete site-specific association, not an interaction adjustment that must be interpreted alone.

text: Three-class model-check architecture Hard failure was reserved for an unavailable or non-estimable base result, convergence or Hessian failure, singularity, rank or covariance failure, invalid timing support, observed-response support failure, or visually confirmed gross residual behavior. Residual distribution was judged visually from residual-versus-fitted and Q–Q displays for Gaussian or HC3 fits. Tweedie fits used Pearson residual-versus-fitted displays and zero-mass and prediction- support checks; normal Pearson residuals were not required. All 468 non-L10 metric-by-predictor-by-scenario cells had complete visual review and no gross visual or hard construct failure after the gap clock-unit repair. Each was retained as acceptable with limitations. Autocorrelation, participant or site deletion, exact-period, and response-family checks are mandatory row-linked sidecars. They qualify interpretation but do not by themselves fail an otherwise estimable result. text: Exploratory 30-minute clock-time GAMM The clock-time analysis has a different row and estimand. Its outcome Y is the arithmetic mean melEDI in an admissible 30-minute bin. The displayed inverse transform, 10^\eta - 0.1 , is a back-transform of the conditional mean log response. It is geometric-mean-like for Y+0.1 and is not raw-scale arithmetic E[Y] . title: H07: Photoperiod and qualifying transitions in personal light exposure – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Scientific question The preregistered hypothesis was: “H7: There is a ceiling (nonlinear) effect of absolute latitude and photoperiod on level-, duration-, and exposure-history-based light metrics.” Melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance (melEDI) is an illuminance-like measure weighted for melanopic photoreception and expressed in lux (lx). The primary near-eye sensor position places the wearable sensor near the eyes; the complementary chest sensor position is torso-worn and is not a measure of ocular exposure. This report asks the part of that question that these data can address: is a pooled association between civil photoperiod and each planned personal light-exposure metric visible, and does the fitted association change from a locally supported increase to a slope that remains statistically compatible with zero through the longest recorded photoperiod? Note Answer in brief A qualifying transition from increase to a sustained near-flat tail was visible for six of nine primary near-eye metrics : mean melEDI, brightest 10 h mean, darkest 10 h mean, time above 1,000 lx melEDI, time above 250 lx melEDI during wake, and melEDI dose. Their transition brackets ranged from 14.24–16.20 h of civil photoperiod. The complementary chest analysis showed the pattern for seven of nine metrics : mean melEDI, darkest 10 h mean, both above-threshold durations, time below 1 lx melEDI during sleep, the longest continuous period above 250 lx melEDI, and melEDI dose. Their transition brackets ranged from 13.01–18.47 h. These are visible pooled-data patterns under the qualifying-transition rule, not evidence that a physiological or environmental ceiling exists. No physiological or environmental ceiling was identified. Absolute latitude cannot be separated from site in this design, and site, collection period, incomplete photoperiod overlap, model form, and influential sites materially limit interpretation.

title: H07: Photoperiod and qualifying transitions in personal light exposure – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
section: Data, sensor positions, metrics, and support
text: Data, sensor positions, metrics, and support All nine planned metrics were analysed independently of fitted results from other hypotheses. Near-eye measurements are primary because they more closely represent light near the eyes; chest measurements provide complementary evidence. The placements were modelled separately. A common-sample sensitivity uses the same participants and participant-days for both placements, but it does not test or establish placement equivalence. The primary dataset retains the approved metric-specific treatment of gaps. A predefined sensitivity uses the gap-timing-unaware dataset . It still passed the general 50%-per-hour and 80%-per-day coverage rules. The term means that the timing of the remaining missing observations is not used for an additional metric-specific adjustment; it does not mean that gaps, missingness, or coverage were ignored. For this contrast only, the approved primary preparation could be interpreted as a time-sensitive primary metric dataset , because it uses the timing of remaining missing observations where that timing is relevant to the metric. Below, it is called simply the primary dataset. A participant-day is one participant’s available metric value on one local calendar date at one sensor position. Repeated days were handled with a participant random-effect smooth nested within site. Depending on the metric, the primary near-eye analysis contains 139–141 participants and 655–816 participant-days, whereas the complementary chest analysis contains 153–154 participants and 743–902 participant-days. The recorded civil-photoperiod support used by the metric-specific fits spans 10.33–20.52 h overall. The main near-eye samples span 15 August 2023 to 19 October 2025; chest samples span 14 May 2024 to 19 October 2025. Exact metric-specific counts are reported with each placement below. title: H07: Photoperiod and qualifying transitions in personal light exposure – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Reading guide A nonlinear generalized additive model (GAM) analysis allows the association between civil photoperiod and a light metric to bend rather than follow a straight line. The resulting line is called the fitted curve. The derivative is the slope of that fitted curve: how quickly the fitted outcome changes for each additional hour of photoperiod at each point. Here it is evaluated on the model’s linear-predictor scale, in model-scale units per hour; the left-hand fitted curves are displayed in the named metric units. A pointwise 95% confidence interval (95% CI) describes uncertainty at one photoperiod value. It is not a simultaneous uncertainty band for the whole curve. Overlap among nonlinear model terms can make their separate contributions harder to distinguish. This is reported below using the technical term concurvity .

title: H07: Photoperiod and qualifying transitions in personal light exposure – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
section: Nonlinear photoperiod model and qualifying-transition rule
text: Nonlinear photoperiod model and qualifying-transition rule Each metric and placement used a separate nonlinear GAM fitted by restricted maximum likelihood. The reported model was: Show R code formula_registry |> filter (.data $ model_id == "adapted_photoperiod_smooth" ) |> pull (.data $ formula) |> cat () response_value ~ s(photoperiod_hours, k = 6, bs = “tp”) + s(site, bs = “re”) + s(site_participant, bs = “re”) Here, response_value is the response shown in the specification table, photoperiod_hours is civil photoperiod, site is the study site, and site_participant identifies a participant within site. The smooth used a thin-plate regression spline with basis dimension k = 6. A broader k = 10 smooth and a model treating site as a fixed effect were fitted as model-form sensitivities. Absolute latitude is fixed within site. It is therefore structurally confounded with site, and a latitude-by-photoperiod surface cannot separately identify a latitude association while accounting for site. The planned joint surface was inspected as an identifiability check but is not used for inference or for the qualifying-transition classification. No temperature or other unplanned environmental predictor was added. For each reported smooth, the first derivative was evaluated at 100 equally spaced values over that metric’s exact recorded photoperiod range. Central finite differences used a step of 0.01 h, with one-sided differences at the two boundaries. Unconditional model-coefficient covariance produced pointwise 95% confidence intervals on the model’s linear-predictor scale. A qualifying transition from increase to a sustained near-flat tail 1 required all three conditions: the immediately preceding grid point had a derivative interval wholly above zero; the next grid point had a derivative interval containing zero; and every later grid point through the longest recorded photoperiod also had a zero-compatible derivative interval. The reported transition is the bracket from the last pointwise detected increase to the first point of the sustained zero-compatible tail. This is the requested change from a statistically supported positive derivative to a non-significant derivative that remains non-significant to the end of the recorded range. The rule does not define a scientifically negligible slope, prove equivalence to zero, locate a true asymptote, or demonstrate a mechanism. The 100 pointwise checks and the nine cross-metric classifications were not multiplicity-adjusted; the classification is therefore descriptive.

title: H07: Photoperiod and qualifying transitions in personal light exposure – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Model checks All 18 reported models converged. Gradients were small and all reported Hessian minima were positive. Residual autocorrelation means that observations close in sequence retain more similar residuals than observations farther apart. Consecutive-day residual autocorrelation was modest in the pooled descriptive check, with maximum absolute lag-1 correlations of 0.229 near eye and 0.154 at the chest. This does not prove temporal independence, but it did not indicate a strong residual day-to-day process after participant clustering. Table 6: Summary of convergence, smooth-basis, temporal, overlap among nonlinear terms (concurvity), and residual model checks. Converged Maximum absolute gradient Minimum Hessian eigenvalue Basis flags of 9 Maximum |lag 1| Photoperiod/participant concurvity Deviance explained QQ correlation range Near eye — primary 9/9 0.0014 0.00002 3 0.2287 0.9986–0.9988 40.7%–65.6% 0.952–0.998 Chest — complementary 9/9 0.0009 0.00020 1 0.1542 0.9985–0.9987 33.6%–57.6% 0.960–0.996 The basis-dimension check flagged three near-eye smooths and one chest smooth. The expanded-basis sensitivity therefore carries more weight than a single diagnostic threshold: it reproduced 16 of 17 evaluable classifications, with one near-eye fit failing its Hessian check and the chest sleep low-light classification changing. Residual normal-reference correlations were generally high, but residuals still showed fitted-value dependence and tail departures for some outcomes. The Tweedie response checks were adequate for the two above-threshold duration metrics. They were not adequate for time below 1 lx melEDI during sleep: each placement had four observed zeros, the fitted model expected fewer than 0.0001 zeros, and none of 100 pilot simulations contained a zero. This distributional mismatch makes the chest sleep low-light pattern particularly weak evidence; no larger simulation can repair the response model’s failure to reproduce the observed zero mass. The photoperiod smooth also had estimated overlap with the participant random-effect smooth (concurvity) of approximately 0.9985–0.9988. This reflects the clustered, repeated-day design and makes their separate contributions harder to distinguish. It limits separation of between-person photoperiod coverage from the pooled smooth. Smooth-term p-values are therefore not used or displayed. The derivative intervals remain conditional on the fitted model and should be read with this identifiability limitation.

text: Sensitivity analyses Each sensitivity changed a named feature. The gap-timing-unaware dataset omitted the additional metric-specific adjustment based on when remaining gaps occurred while retaining the coverage rules. The paired/common analysis used only participant-days available at both sensor positions. The cross-dataset common-row analyses restricted the primary and gap-timing-unaware definitions to identical rows. The longest-period analysis retained only days with an exactly identified period, and the dose analysis compared observed and corrected melEDI dose on identical rows. Model-form sensitivities increased photoperiod-smooth flexibility from k = 6 to k = 10 or represented site with fixed rather than random effects. Leave-one-site-out analyses omitted one named site at a time. Agreement below concerns the yes/no qualifying-transition classification, not an identical transition point. The gap-timing-unaware dataset reproduced all nine near-eye classifications and eight of nine chest classifications; the chest melEDI-dose pattern was the exception. The paired common sample used 110–112 participants, 505–643 participant-days and observations, and eight sites. title: H07: Photoperiod and qualifying transitions in personal light exposure – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Interpretation and limitations The pooled analysis shows several fitted photoperiod associations that rise and then meet the prespecified pointwise rule for a sustained zero-compatible derivative. The recurring patterns for mean melEDI, darkest 10 h mean, both above-threshold duration metrics, and melEDI dose across the two placements are the most consistent descriptive findings. Brightest 10 h mean differs by placement, the longest-period result is sensitive to sample definition and model form, and the chest sleep low-light result is undermined by distributional failure, common-row analyses, model-form changes, and site influence. The strongest defensible conclusion is therefore that qualifying transitions from increase to a sustained near-flat tail are visible for several personal light-exposure metrics in the pooled data , subject to substantial design and model limitations. The results do not establish a ceiling, an equivalence region, a causal effect of photoperiod, a distinct latitude effect, a health or clinical consequence, or equivalence between near-eye and chest placement.

title: H07 analysis preparation and provenance – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Scientific target This companion documents the analysis underlying the H07 results report . The result report’s preregistration-deviation section provides reciprocal navigation to the current scientific deviations. The preregistered hypothesis was: “H7: There is a ceiling (nonlinear) effect of absolute latitude and photoperiod on level-, duration-, and exposure-history-based light metrics.” Melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance (melEDI) is an illuminance-like measure weighted for melanopic photoreception and expressed in lux (lx). The primary near-eye sensor position places the wearable sensor near the eyes; the complementary chest sensor position is torso-worn and is not ocular exposure. A participant-day is one participant’s metric value on one local calendar date at one sensor position. A nonlinear generalized additive model (GAM) analysis allows the photoperiod association to bend rather than follow a straight line. The derivative is the slope of the fitted curve: the change in the fitted outcome for each additional hour of photoperiod at each point. H07 evaluates it on the model’s linear-predictor scale, in model-scale units per hour. A pointwise 95% confidence interval (95% CI) describes uncertainty at one photoperiod value; it is not a simultaneous band for the whole curve. Overlap among nonlinear model terms makes their separate contributions harder to distinguish; the technical term for this is concurvity . The design cannot separate absolute latitude from site, because each site has one latitude. The estimable target is therefore narrower: for each of nine planned metrics and each placement, describe the pooled association with civil photoperiod and ask whether the fitted smooth changes from a pointwise detected increase to a first derivative whose pointwise interval contains zero at every remaining grid point through the longest recorded photoperiod. This is a qualifying transition from increase to a sustained near-flat tail. 1 It is not an equivalence test and does not establish a physiological or environmental ceiling.

text: Metrics, units, and response construction All nine planned metrics enter independently. Reader-facing names use melEDI and “period.” Internal identifiers are retained only for reproducibility. Definitions and derivations are documented in Preparation 04 . title: H07 analysis preparation and provenance – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Temporal order and repeated participant-days Dates are local calendar dates. Civil photoperiod is joined by site and local date. Frames are ordered by site, participant, and date before fitting. Participants contribute repeated days, so each model contains a random-effect smooth for participant nested within site. Site also has its own random-effect smooth. One participant-day contributes only one row per metric and placement; there is no within-day residual time series in H07. No independent temperature, season, or collection-period predictor is added. Season and collection period remain embedded in the observed date and photoperiod pattern. Consecutive-day residual correlations are descriptive checks of remaining temporal dependence rather than a fitted autocorrelation structure.

text: Association and derivative estimands The association estimand is the fitted pooled civil-photoperiod smooth for one metric and placement, conditional on the model structure. Response-scale curves are used for scientific display: when a response was transformed for fitting, the fitted quantity was converted back to the displayed metric unit. The derivative estimand underlying the qualifying transition is the first derivative of that smooth on the model’s linear-predictor scale per hour of civil photoperiod. For each metric and placement, derivatives are evaluated at 100 equally spaced points from the exact minimum to maximum recorded photoperiod. Central finite differences use an increment of 0.01 h; the lower boundary uses a forward difference and the upper boundary a backward difference. The pointwise 95% interval uses the unconditional covariance matrix. A pattern is present only when: the immediately preceding grid point has a derivative interval wholly above zero; the next point has a derivative interval containing zero; and every later point through the recorded maximum also has an interval containing zero. The transition is bracketed by the preceding and current grid points. A non-significant derivative at one point, a visual flattening, or an AIC threshold is not sufficient. The rule has no scientifically defensible equivalence margin, no simultaneous curve band, and no curve-wide or cross-metric multiplicity adjustment. It therefore supports only a pointwise, descriptive qualifying-transition classification, not a ceiling claim. No p-value enters the reported qualifying-transition classification. text: Model checks and support limits All 18 reported photoperiod-smooth fits converged. Four smooths—three near-eye and one chest—met the recorded basis-dimension flag criterion, motivating the broader-basis sensitivity. Estimated overlap among nonlinear model terms (concurvity) supplied by the nested participant smooth to the photoperiod smooth was approximately 0.9985–0.9988. This is the principal identifiability limitation: the pooled photoperiod shape is difficult to separate from which participants contribute at which photoperiods. Show the R code used for this display diagnostic_summary |> mutate ( Placement = unname (placement_labels[.data $ placement]) ) |> transmute ( .data $ Placement, ` Fitted models ` = .data $ fitted_models, Converged = .data $ converged_models, ` Basis flags ` = .data $ basis_dimension_flags, ` Participant concurvity ` = format_range ( .data $ minimum_participant_concurvity, .data $ maximum_participant_concurvity, digits = 4 ), ` Maximum |consecutive-day lag 1| ` = .data $ maximum_absolute_consecutive_day_lag1 ) |> gt :: gt ( rowname_col = "Placement" ) |> gt :: fmt_integer ( columns = c ( ` Fitted models ` , Converged, ` Basis flags ` )) |> gt :: fmt_number ( columns = ` Maximum |consecutive-day lag 1| ` , decimals = 3 ) |> prep_gt () Table 12: Summary of convergence, basis, overlap among nonlinear terms (concurvity), and temporal model checks Fitted models Converged Basis flags Participant concurvity Maximum |consecutive-day lag 1| Chest — complementary 9 9 1 0.9985–0.9987 0.154 Near eye — primary 9 9 3 0.9986–0.9988 0.229 Residual summaries retained fitted-value dependence and tail checks for every metric. Residual autocorrelation means that observations close in sequence retain more similar residuals than observations farther apart. Consecutive-day lag-1 correlations did not cross the prespecified 0.30 descriptive warning threshold, but that does not prove temporal independence. Three metrics use a Tweedie response. A frozen 100-draw pilot checked zero mass and positive-tail behaviour. The two above-threshold duration metrics were broadly compatible with the fitted distributions. For time below 1 lx melEDI during sleep, each placement had four observed zeros, the analytic expected count was below 0.0001, and none of the 100 pilot draws contained a zero. This distributional failure weakens any pattern for that metric; more simulation cannot repair the model’s inability to reproduce the observed zero mass. title: H08: Visual light sensitivity and personal light exposure – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Scientific question The Visual Light Sensitivity Questionnaire (VLSQ-8) measures self-reported visual light sensitivity; higher scores indicate greater sensitivity according to the accepted scale. The preregistered hypothesis was: H8: Duration-, exposure-history-, and level-based metrics are associated with VLSQ-8 light sensitivity scores. The analytical question is whether VLSQ-8 is associated with repeated participant-day personal light-exposure metrics after adjustment for study site. A participant-day is one participant’s eligible local calendar day. The primary near-eye sensor position more closely represents light near the eyes during wear. The complementary chest sensor position is not an ocular-exposure measure and is not pooled with near-eye measurements. Melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance (melEDI) describes light in terms of melanopsin-weighted visual-system sensitivity. Reported effects compare VLSQ-8 scores separated by one participant-level standard deviation (SD) , equal to 5.540 points. Time below 10 lx melEDI before sleep is reported as an absolute difference in hours; the eight log-link outcomes are reported as ratios and corresponding percentage changes, on a separate scale. A back-transformed estimate returns a fitted coefficient to its stated hour-difference, ratio, or percentage-change scale. A 95% confidence interval (95% CI) describes the uncertainty around that effect; Wald construction is named where relevant. The site-average association is an average across sites that gives each site equal weight. The separate VLSQ-8-by-site interaction allows the association between VLSQ-8 and a light metric to differ by study site. False-discovery-rate (FDR) adjustment is applied within each declared nine-metric family. Note Answer in brief Across nine light-exposure metrics, neither the primary near-eye site-average associations nor their VLSQ-8-by-site interactions met the FDR-adjusted criterion. The strongest near-eye directional pattern was lower corrected melEDI dose per VLSQ-8 SD (ratio 0.846, 95% CI 0.716–0.999; raw p = 0.051, FDR-adjusted p = 0.160), so it is not an FDR-retained finding. Complementary chest results and the central sensitivity analyses did not change that conclusion, although site influence and specified model limitations require caution.

title: H08: Visual light sensitivity and personal light exposure – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
section: Score, sensor positions, and light-exposure metrics
text: Score, sensor positions, and light-exposure metrics VLSQ-8 was available for all 184 participants across nine sites. The stored score equalled the sum of eight ordered 1–5 item codes plus 5 for every participant. Scores ranged from 13 to 39, with a mean of 21.598 and a participant SD of 5.540. The raw score was centred at the observed mean; no within-site standardisation was used. Nine participant-day outcomes covered light level, duration, continuous periods, and exposure history. All use manuscript metric names and melEDI units. Current definitions are documented in Preparation 04 , and the model-ready inputs in Preparation 06 . The longest continuous period is an observed lower bound unless its start and end are both exactly identified; that stricter definition is examined as a sensitivity analysis. The predefined preparation sensitivity is called the gap-timing-unaware dataset . It still passed the general 50%-per-hour and 80%-per-day coverage rules. The name means that the timing of the remaining missing observations is not used for an additional metric-specific adjustment; it does not mean that gaps, missingness, or coverage were ignored. For this one-time first explanation, the primary could be interpreted as a time-sensitive primary metric dataset because its approved preparation uses the timing of remaining missing observations where that timing is relevant. From here onward, it is called simply the primary dataset . Table 1: H08 light-exposure metrics, response specifications, and reported effect scales. title: H08: Visual light sensitivity and personal light exposure – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Primary near-eye results None of the nine average near-eye associations remained statistically supported after the complete FDR adjustment. Several point estimates suggested lower bright-light exposure at higher VLSQ-8 scores, but their uncertainty and family-adjusted evidence do not support a confirmatory claim. The corrected melEDI-dose ratio was 0.846 per VLSQ-8 SD (95% CI 0.716–0.999). Its likelihood-ratio raw p was 0.051 and FDR-adjusted p was 0.160. The Wald interval and likelihood-ratio test use different inferential constructions; the complete-family conclusion is therefore inconclusive, not statistically significant. title: H08: Visual light sensitivity and personal light exposure – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Interpretation On the accepted score, metric, sample, and model definitions, the observed data provide no FDR-adjusted evidence that VLSQ-8 score is associated with any of the nine primary near-eye personal light-exposure metrics. The complementary chest analyses and the central sensitivity analyses do not materially strengthen that evidence. Several estimates point toward lower bright-light exposure at higher scores, but their uncertainty, complete-family adjustment, and site influence make that directional pattern inconclusive. This conclusion is not evidence that every true association is exactly zero, and the paired-placement comparison is not an equivalence test. The analysis is observational: it does not establish that visual light sensitivity changes personal light exposure, nor does it support physiological or health-effect claims.

text: H08 analysis preparation and provenance Show All Code Hide All Code View Source From verified Visual Light Sensitivity Questionnaire (VLSQ-8) scores and personal light-exposure metrics to reported associations Last modified: August 12, 2026 Note About this analysis record This page explains how verified Visual Light Sensitivity Questionnaire (VLSQ-8) scores and personal light-exposure metrics were turned into the H08 results. Higher VLSQ-8 scores indicate greater self-reported visual light sensitivity according to the accepted scale. The companion H08 results report presents the scientific findings.

title: H08 analysis preparation and provenance – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Purpose H08 asks whether nine duration-, exposure-history-, and level-based personal light-exposure metrics are associated with VLSQ-8 visual-light-sensitivity scores. The primary near-eye sensor position more closely represents light near the eyes during wear. The complementary chest sensor position is not an ocular-exposure measure and is not pooled with near-eye measurement. Melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance (melEDI) expresses light in terms of melanopsin-weighted visual-system sensitivity. Every inferential outcome has one row per participant-day , defined as one participant’s eligible local calendar day. Reported effects compare VLSQ-8 scores separated by one participant-level standard deviation (SD) , equal to 5.540 points. Time below 10 lx melEDI before sleep is reported as an absolute difference in hours; the other eight log-link outcomes use ratios and corresponding percentage changes. A back-transformed estimate returns a fitted coefficient to its stated hour difference, ratio, or percentage-change scale. A 95% confidence interval (95% CI) describes uncertainty; Wald construction is named where relevant. The site-average association averages across sites with equal weight. The separate VLSQ-8-by-site interaction allows the association between VLSQ-8 and a light metric to differ by site. False-discovery-rate (FDR) adjustment is applied within each declared complete nine-metric family. The predefined preparation sensitivity uses the gap-timing-unaware dataset . It still passed the general requirement of at least 50% valid minutes per hour and at least 80% valid hours per day, but the timing of the remaining missing observations was not used for an additional metric-specific adjustment. For contrast at this first explanation, the primary could be interpreted as a time-sensitive primary metric dataset . Hereafter it is called simply the primary dataset. This page identifies the exact data, score rule, samples, formulae, code, and stored checks behind the accepted report. It documents provenance; it does not create an alternate analysis.

section: Schema, key, content, and value checks

title: H08 analysis preparation and provenance – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Scale and score reconstruction VLSQ-8 contains eight ordered item codes from 1 to 5. For every participant, the stored score equalled the item sum plus 5. The constant offset does not affect a centred slope, but retaining it is necessary to reproduce the approved 13–39 score scale. All 184 participants had complete item and total scores. title: H08 analysis preparation and provenance – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Metric definitions and missing values The nine outcomes retain the manuscript names and melEDI units. Unsupported values remain missing; they are never converted to darkness or zero. Four metrics use Gaussian models after log10(value + 0.1) transformation, three non-negative duration metrics use Tweedie models with a log link, and two use Gaussian identity models. Practical effects are ratios except for time below 10 lx melEDI before sleep, which is an hour difference. Current metric derivations are documented in Preparation 04 , and the corresponding model-ready inputs in Preparation 06 . The longest continuous period above 250 lx melEDI can be a lower bound when a remaining gap interrupts the observed period. A separate exact-identification sensitivity retains only participant-days for which both ends of the longest period are observed. The corrected melEDI dose uses the registered time-sensitive value; observed uncorrected dose is retained as a descriptive sensitivity on the same fitted sample. text: 4. Model construction and inference

title: H08 analysis preparation and provenance – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
section: Exact formulae supplied to the models
text: Exact formulae supplied to the models The primary specification uses fixed site with sum-to-zero contrasts and a participant random intercept nested within site. This participant random effect represents remaining between-participant variation after site and VLSQ-8 are considered. The additive coefficient is therefore the site-average VLSQ-8 slope rather than a slope at one reference site. A likelihood-ratio comparison of the site-only and additive models tests the site-average association. Comparing the additive and interaction models tests the VLSQ-8-by-site interaction. Photoperiod adjustment and participant-level summary models are structured sensitivities. This separation is the current scientific choice recorded as DEV-035 . The table retains the exact evaluated Wilkinson formulae used for the current analysis and its two structured sensitivity branches. title: H08 analysis preparation and provenance – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: 5. Model checks and influence Every current additive and interaction fit was checked for convergence, Hessian status, singularity, fixed-effect rank, residual behaviour, response support, prediction bounds, and serial dependence. Exact response zeros and the expected zero mass were compared for Tweedie outcomes. The checks retain three explicit limitations: increasing residual spread for darkest 10 h mean, a small observed zero mass not reproduced for sleep time below 1 lx melEDI, and corrected-dose sensitivity to remaining-gap timing. text: 6. Sensitivity analyses Sensitivity branches preserve the accepted estimand unless their purpose explicitly changes sample construction, adjustment, or metric definition. They describe stability and do not promote an association that was not retained in the primary multiplicity family. For the paired-placement and exact common-sample comparisons, the same participants and participant-days are used at both sensor positions, while near-eye and chest estimates are fitted separately. These are not equivalence tests or direct tests of a placement effect. text: Current numerical-zero evidence The shared METRIC-011 decision normalised eight primary-dataset Darkest 10 h mean participant-day values from the floating-point remnant 4.163336342344337e-17 lx to exact zero: three near-eye and five chest cells. The bounded maintenance rebuilt only the six primary-dataset L10 model branches that inherited those cells, four specified sensitivity bundles, 17 leave-one-site-out fits, and the four affected complete FDR families. No resampling or full-analysis rerun was performed. title: H08 analysis preparation and provenance – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Reproduction guidance A reader can follow the analysis in six passes: inspect the METRIC-011 decision, shared evidence manifest, H08 result comparison, and protected-scope reconciliation for the exact-zero maintenance boundary; inspect H08_input_audit.csv , h08_contract.R , and the score, metric, formula, and run registries to verify frozen inputs and specifications; compare the exact samples above with H08_model_frame_index.csv and the 108 frames in H08_model_frames.rds ; follow run_h08_stage2.R through h08_modeling.R to connect each frame to its stored object, practical effect, 95% interval, likelihood-ratio test, diagnostic, and sensitivity record; inspect all eight complete nine-value multiplicity families before interpreting an individual association; and read the H08 results report alongside its numerical tables, accessible figures, and exact source CSV files. This preparation record documents a frozen analysis. If an input, score rule, metric definition, sample rule, response model, or estimand changes, the affected scientific pipeline must be rerun before this page is refreshed.

text: H09: Chronotype and timing of personal light exposure MCTQ and MEQ associations with five registered timing metrics Last modified: August 12, 2026

title: H09: Chronotype and timing of personal light exposure – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Hypothesis and analytical question The preregistered hypothesis was: H9: Timing-based metrics are associated with chronotype (MCTQ, MEQ). Chronotype was represented by the Munich Chronotype Questionnaire corrected midsleep on free days (MCTQ MSFsc) and the Morningness–Eveningness Questionnaire (MEQ) . The analytical question is whether either construct is associated with the local clock timing of personal light exposure across repeated participant-days after accounting for study site. A participant-day is one participant’s eligible outcome on one local date. The primary sensor position was near eye because it records light near the eyes during wear. The complementary chest sensor position was analysed separately and is not a measure of ocular exposure. Light intensity is expressed as melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance (melEDI) . Effects are signed local-clock hours per stated increase in the chronotype score: positive values mean the timing outcome occurs later and negative values mean earlier. Because larger MCTQ MSFsc means later corrected midsleep while larger MEQ means greater morning preference, the two score directions must be read separately. Note Answer in brief Later MCTQ corrected midsleep was associated with later primary near-eye M10 midpoint, L10 midpoint, and first timing above 250 lx melEDI; greater MEQ morning preference was associated with earlier timing for the same outcomes. These conclusions use separate five-outcome false-discovery-rate (FDR) families. Uncertainty is reported with 95% confidence intervals (95% CIs). The clearest near-eye estimate was for first timing above 250 lx melEDI: +0.381 h per one-hour later MCTQ MSFsc (95% CI +0.146 to +0.616; FDR-adjusted p = 0.003) and −0.444 h per 10 points greater MEQ morning preference (95% CI −0.699 to −0.189; FDR-adjusted p = 0.001). Last timing and the midpoint of the longest continuous period were not supported. Complementary chest results broadly reinforced the first-timing pattern, and no chronotype-by-site interaction survived FDR adjustment. Structured sensitivity analyses supported the main directional interpretation, with explicit limitations for the unavailable longest-period dataset sensitivity and a few near-zero or precision-sensitive estimates.

title: H09: Chronotype and timing of personal light exposure – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Chronotype constructs and timing outcomes MCTQ MSFsc and MEQ represent related but distinct constructs. A larger MCTQ MSFsc value denotes later corrected midsleep, whereas a larger MEQ score denotes greater morning preference. The verified aggregate calculated fields covered 186 participants. MCTQ MSFsc was complete for 185 participants and missing for one; MEQ was complete for all 186. The aggregate values were preserved exactly from their source, but item-level questionnaire responses were unavailable for independent score reconstruction. The five registered participant-day outcomes were the midpoint of the brightest 10 hours (M10 midpoint) , midpoint of the darkest 10 hours (L10 midpoint) , first time above 250 lx melEDI , last time above 250 lx melEDI , and midpoint of the longest continuous period above 250 lx melEDI . M10 and L10 onset and offset were not analysed. Clock values were linearized because their observed support was adequately linear; night-time values used the specified negative-hour conversion where needed. No circular distribution was imposed solely because an outcome was clock-valued. The timing definitions and their support rules are documented in Preparation 04 and the model-ready fields in Preparation 06 . Table 1: Registered H09 timing outcomes. Metric Unit Analysis unit Definition Midpoint of the brightest 10 hours local clock hour participant day Local midpoint of the brightest supported 10 hours Midpoint of the darkest 10 hours local clock hour participant day Local midpoint of the darkest supported 10 hours; strict >16:00 values shifted by -24 hours First light timing above 250 lx melEDI local clock hour participant day First supported local timing above 250 lx melEDI Last light timing above 250 lx melEDI local clock hour participant day Last supported local timing above 250 lx melEDI Midpoint of the longest continuous period above 250 lx melEDI local clock hour participant day Local midpoint of the selected longest continuous period above 250 lx melEDI, restricted to exact-identifiable periods The gap-timing-unaware dataset is the dataset applying the 50%-per-hour and 80%-per-day coverage rules but not using the remaining gaps’ time of day in metric-specific support decisions. It can be contrasted once with the time-sensitive primary dataset; below, the latter is called simply the primary dataset.

title: H09: Chronotype and timing of personal light exposure – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Statistical approach Each chronotype instrument was analysed separately. Participant-day Gaussian mixed models included fixed study-site effects and a participant random effect nested within site. This random effect represents remaining between-participant timing variation after site and chronotype are considered. The additive model estimated a study-site-adjusted average between-participant association and was compared with a site-only model. A separate chronotype-by-site interaction model allowed the chronotype association to differ by study site. Site-specific slopes were treated as descriptive unless the global interaction survived FDR adjustment. Table 2: Exact Wilkinson formulas used for the principal H09 comparisons. Instrument Role Formula MCTQ MSFsc Site only timing_hour ~ site + (1 | site:Id) MCTQ MSFsc Average chronotype association timing_hour ~ site + mctq_hour_centered + (1 | site:Id) MCTQ MSFsc Chronotype-by-site interaction timing_hour ~ site * mctq_hour_centered + (1 | site:Id) MEQ Site only timing_hour ~ site + (1 | site:Id) MEQ Average chronotype association timing_hour ~ site + meq_10_centered + (1 | site:Id) MEQ Chronotype-by-site interaction timing_hour ~ site * meq_10_centered + (1 | site:Id) The centered predictor names encode simple changes of origin and scale. mctq_hour_centered is each participant’s MCTQ MSFsc expressed in clock hours minus the participant mean (4.114 h); an increase of one unit therefore means one hour later corrected midsleep. meq_10_centered is the MEQ score minus the participant mean (52.860) and divided by 10; an increase of one unit means 10 MEQ points toward greater morning preference. Centering places the model intercept at the observed mean chronotype. It does not change the chronotype slopes, their confidence intervals, or their tests. Each coefficient is a signed-hour estimand. Positive values mean the timing outcome occurs later per one-hour later MCTQ MSFsc or per 10 points greater MEQ morning preference; negative values mean earlier. The different score directions are therefore retained in every interpretation. Four inferential families were kept distinct for each placement: MCTQ average associations, MEQ average associations, MCTQ-by-site interactions, and MEQ-by-site interactions. Each complete family used FDR adjustment across the five registered timing outcomes. Statistical significance was decided at FDR-adjusted p < 0.050 before formatting. All displayed intervals are 95% Wald CIs. The mean-timing sensitivity reported later was not added to these families.

title: H09: Chronotype and timing of personal light exposure – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
section: Model checks, dependence, influence, and limitations
text: Model checks, dependence, influence, and limitations The model-check registry (model diagnostics) assessed 16 domains for each of 24 primary targets. Eighteen targets were acceptable across every domain; six retained at least one explicit limitation. Visual review of the full near-eye and chest panels supported acceptable final assessments for response/residual distribution and residual heteroscedasticity. Conservative numerical screen flags remain in the model-check source data and are not erased by that visual assessment. Table 8: Primary targets retaining at least one explicit model-check limitation. Placement Metric Instrument Retained limitation(s) Participants / days / observations / hours / sites Near eye Last light timing above 250 lx melEDI MCTQ Participant influence ; Site influence 140 / 683 / 683 / 15900.8 h / 9 Near eye Last light timing above 250 lx melEDI MEQ Participant influence ; Site influence 141 / 687 / 687 / 15995.0 h / 9 Chest Midpoint of the longest continuous period above 250 lx melEDI MCTQ Prepared-data sensitivity 149 / 547 / 547 / 12980.0 h / 8 Near eye Midpoint of the longest continuous period above 250 lx melEDI MCTQ Prepared-data sensitivity 131 / 478 / 478 / 11325.5 h / 9 Chest Midpoint of the longest continuous period above 250 lx melEDI MEQ Convergence and Hessian ; Singularity and variance ; Prepared-data sensitivity 150 / 549 / 549 / 13027.8 h / 8 Near eye Midpoint of the longest continuous period above 250 lx melEDI MEQ Prepared-data sensitivity 132 / 482 / 482 / 11419.8 h / 9 Distribution and heteroscedasticity are not among these final limitations. A target can have more than one remaining domain. The two near-eye last-timing slopes were close to zero and changed direction under some participant-deletion and leave-one-site-out checks, although no deletion changed a slope by the material 0.25-hour threshold. Chest longest-period/MEQ had a singular maximum-likelihood chronotype-by-site interaction fit; its additive main-effect fit remained estimable, but that interaction fit remains a model-check limitation. The registered longest-period outcome was unavailable in the gap-timing-unaware prepared artifact at both placements and for both instruments. Fixed-effect matrices were full rank and Hessians positive definite for all stored fits. Repeated observations closer in time may retain more similar residuals, a dependence called autocorrelation. A continuous-time first-order autoregressive, or AR(1), sensitivity represented this dependence as stronger at shorter elapsed-time gaps; its corrections changed slopes by at most 0.016 h. Figure 3: Near-eye residual-versus-fitted and normal-score Q-Q model checks for the six analysed timing outcomes and both chronotype instruments. Visual review supported acceptable response/residual distribution and heteroscedasticity assessments. Figure 4: Chest residual-versus-fitted and normal-score Q-Q model checks for the six analysed timing outcomes and both chronotype instruments. Visual review supported acceptable response/residual distribution and heteroscedasticity assessments. The complete model-check registry , residual-check assessment record , participant-influence summary , and leave-one-site-out summary retain the thresholds, evidence, and final assessment basis.

title: H09: Chronotype and timing of personal light exposure – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Dataset sensitivity For these comparisons, a common sample means that the primary and gap-timing-unaware datasets use the same participants and participant-days. For the four registered outcomes available in both datasets, the models were compared on those identical participant-day keys. Fifteen of 16 instrument-by-placement comparisons were stable within model uncertainty. Chest MCTQ L10 was precision-sensitive, with overlapping 95% intervals but a change in whether the interval excluded zero. The registered longest-period midpoint could not be evaluated because the gap-timing-unaware artifact contains neither that metric nor the endpoints needed to derive it. title: H09: Chronotype and timing of personal light exposure – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Other named sensitivity analyses The photoperiod sensitivity added centered within-site photoperiod to the participant-day model. It was stable for 21 of 24 targets; its two direction-sensitive results were the near-zero near-eye last-timing slopes, and one chest mean-timing estimate was precision-sensitive. The participant summary sensitivity replaced repeated participant-day outcomes with one equal-weight outcome mean per participant; it was stable for 20 of 24 targets, with direction changes confined to near-zero last-timing or chest longest-period slopes. All 24 continuous-time AR(1) checks of residual autocorrelation were stable. The L10 clock-cut sensitivity compared the registered strict >16:00 negative-hour conversion with a noon cut; slopes changed by at most 0.037 h, and all four checks were acceptable. Table 10: Summary of structured sensitivity classifications. Sensitivity Targets assessed Result Within-site photoperiod adjustment 24 21 stable; 2 direction-sensitive; 1 precision-sensitive Equal-weight participant summary 24 20 stable; 4 direction-sensitive Continuous-time AR(1) 24 24 stable; maximum slope change 0.016 h L10 clock cut 4 4 acceptable; maximum slope change 0.037 h The registered fifth outcome remained the midpoint of the longest continuous period. Mean timing across all supported exposure above 250 lx melEDI is a distinct sensitivity estimand and was not substituted for that outcome. Its near-eye MEQ estimate was −0.169 h per 10 MEQ points (95% CI −0.334 to −0.003; raw p = 0.041), but this raw result is outside the registered multiplicity families and does not alter the confirmatory conclusion. title: H09: Chronotype and timing of personal light exposure – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Interpretation The primary near-eye evidence supports an association between chronotype and the timing of several, but not all, features of personal light exposure. Participants with later corrected midsleep tended to have later M10, L10, and first-above-250 timing; participants with greater morning preference tended to show the corresponding earlier timing. The agreement of these distinct chronotype constructs strengthens the directional interpretation without making them interchangeable. The data did not support an association with last-above-250 timing or the registered longest-period midpoint, nor did they support chronotype-by-site interactions after FDR adjustment. Chest evidence was complementary and broadly consistent, but it neither replaces the primary near-eye results nor establishes placement equivalence. The analysis is observational and between participants; it does not establish that chronotype causes a change in personal light exposure timing. The conclusion should be read alongside the direction instability of the near-zero near-eye last-timing estimates, the qualified chest longest-period/MEQ interaction fit, and the unavailable longest-period gap-timing-unaware comparison. These limitations do not change the supported M10, L10, and first-timing pattern, but they constrain claims about the unsupported outcomes and cross-dataset robustness.

DEV-039 : the analysis uses four complete five-outcome FDR families—MCTQ average, MEQ average, MCTQ-by-site interaction, and MEQ-by-site interaction.

title: H09 analysis preparation and provenance – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Purpose This page explains how verified chronotype fields and personal light-exposure timing metrics lead to the scientific findings in the H09 results report . H09 asks whether participant-level chronotype is associated with five participant-day timing metrics of personal light exposure. A participant-day is one participant’s eligible outcome on one local date. Chronotype is represented by the Munich Chronotype Questionnaire corrected midsleep on free days (MCTQ MSFsc) and the Morningness–Eveningness Questionnaire (MEQ) . Larger MCTQ MSFsc means later corrected midsleep, whereas larger MEQ means greater morning preference; the two constructs remain separate in the models and inferential families. Personal light exposure is expressed as melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance (melEDI) . The primary near-eye sensor position records light near the eyes during wear. The complementary chest sensor position is analysed separately, is not pooled with near-eye measurement, and is not a measure of ocular exposure. The gap-timing-unaware dataset is the dataset applying the 50%-per-hour and 80%-per-day coverage rules but not using the remaining gaps’ time of day in metric-specific support decisions. At this first explanation it can be contrasted with the time-sensitive primary dataset; hereafter the latter is called simply the primary dataset. This page identifies the exact inputs, derived fields, analytical frames, formulae, model checks, sensitivity analyses, outputs, and file identities behind the results. It documents provenance and does not create an additional analysis. Uncertainty is reported as 95% confidence intervals (95% CIs), and multiplicity is handled with false-discovery-rate (FDR) adjustment.

text: Centering and scaling The two model-column names, mctq_hour_centered and meq_10_centered , encode only a change of origin and, for MEQ, a reporting scale: MCTQ: mctq_hour_centered = MCTQ MSFsc in hours - 4.1135843 MEQ: meq_10_centered = (MEQ score - 52.8602151) / 10 Thus one MCTQ unit means one hour later corrected midsleep, while one MEQ unit means 10 score points toward greater morning preference. title: H09 analysis preparation and provenance – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Placement and dataset common samples For the placement comparison, near-eye and chest effects were fitted separately using the same participants and participant-days within each metric and instrument. Their paired component estimates therefore share a sample, but they are not a direct placement-effect or equivalence test; no equivalence margin was prespecified. Primary and gap-timing-unaware effects likewise use the same participants and participant-days—a common sample—where the same estimand exists in both datasets. The registered longest-period midpoint is unavailable in the preparation-sensitivity artifact and is not imputed. section: Exact formulae supplied to the models
text: Exact formulae supplied to the models For each metric, placement, dataset, sample, and chronotype instrument, the site-only model is compared with an additive chronotype model. The additive model estimates the study-site-adjusted average association and includes a participant random effect, which represents remaining between-participant timing variation after site and chronotype are considered. A second comparison adds a chronotype-by-site interaction, allowing the chronotype association to differ by study site. The distinction between these two questions is recorded in DEV-038 . Each coefficient is a signed effect in local clock hours. Positive values mean the timing outcome occurs later per one-hour later MCTQ MSFsc or per 10 points greater MEQ morning preference; negative values mean earlier. Restricted maximum-likelihood additive fits provide coefficients and 95% Wald CIs; maximum-likelihood fits provide the nested likelihood-ratio tests. A natural-spline fit is used only to assess whether the observed predictor support is adequately represented as linear. Show the R code used for this display formula_registry |> filter (.data $ analysis_kind == "approved_participant_day" ) |> mutate ( Role = recode ( .data $ formula_id, M0_site_only = "Site-only comparison model" , M1_main = "Additive chronotype model" , M2_interaction = "Chronotype-by-site interaction model" , D_spline = "Linearity model check" ) ) |> transmute ( Instrument = .data $ instrument, Role, ` Formula supplied ` = .data $ formula ) |> gt :: gt ( groupname_col = "Instrument" ) |> prep_gt ( 9 ) Table 8: Exact stored Wilkinson formulae for the principal models and linearity model check. Role Formula supplied MCTQ Site-only comparison model timing_hour ~ site + (1 | site:Id) Additive chronotype model timing_hour ~ site + mctq_hour_centered + (1 | site:Id) Chronotype-by-site interaction model timing_hour ~ site * mctq_hour_centered + (1 | site:Id) Linearity model check timing_hour ~ site + splines::ns(mctq_hour_centered, df = 3) + (1 | site:Id) MEQ Site-only comparison model timing_hour ~ site + (1 | site:Id) Additive chronotype model timing_hour ~ site + meq_10_centered + (1 | site:Id) Chronotype-by-site interaction model timing_hour ~ site * meq_10_centered + (1 | site:Id) Linearity model check timing_hour ~ site + splines::ns(meq_10_centered, df = 3) + (1 | site:Id) The sensitivity formulae retain the same chronotype definitions. Photoperiod is centered within site and added without an unsupported interaction, and participant-summary models use one outcome mean per participant. Measurements closer in time may retain more similar residuals, a dependence called autocorrelation. Continuous-time first-order autoregressive, or AR(1), fits represent this dependence as stronger at shorter elapsed-time gaps and use elapsed day only for the within-participant correlation structure. text: Multiplicity families FDR adjustment is applied in four separate five-outcome families: MCTQ average associations, MEQ average associations, MCTQ-by-site interactions, and MEQ-by-site interactions. Near-eye, chest, paired, and preparation-sensitivity runs retain separate family instances. Significance is decided from unrounded adjusted values before three-decimal display. Site-specific slopes are descriptive unless the global chronotype-by-site interaction family supports heterogeneity. title: H09 analysis preparation and provenance – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Model checks, influence, and limitations Sixteen model-check domains (model diagnostics) were interpreted for each of 24 primary metric-by-instrument-by-placement targets. Stored checks cover questionnaire provenance, sample and join identity, site support, clock representation, linearity, residual distribution and spread, convergence, singularity, rank, temporal dependence, participant and site influence, placement identity, preparation sensitivity, and multiplicity. Visual inspection of the complete residual panels supported acceptable final response/residual distribution and heteroscedasticity assessments. The quantitative screen values remain stored. Eighteen targets are acceptable across all domains; six retain an influence, interaction-fit, or unavailable preparation-sensitivity limitation. Show the R code used for this display tibble :: tribble ( ~ Record, ~ Targets_or_rows, ~ Acceptable_or_clear, ~ Limitations_or_screen_flags, ~ Interpretation, "Overall target assessment" , nrow (diagnostic_summary), sum (diagnostic_summary $ overall_assessment == "acceptable" ), sum (diagnostic_summary $ overall_assessment == "not acceptable" ), "Final interpreted assessment across 16 domains." , "Integrated distribution check" , nrow (diagnostic_summary), sum (diagnostic_adjudication $ domain == "Response and residual distribution" & diagnostic_adjudication $ numeric_screen_assessment == "acceptable" ), sum (diagnostic_adjudication $ domain == "Response and residual distribution" & diagnostic_adjudication $ numeric_screen_assessment == "not acceptable" ), "Eight conservative screen flags retained; the final visual assessment is acceptable." , "Lower-level distribution screen" , nrow (residual_diagnostics), sum (residual_diagnostics $ distribution_assessment == "acceptable" ), sum (residual_diagnostics $ distribution_assessment == "not acceptable" ), "Fourteen all-threshold flags retained, including outlier-only flags." , "Heteroscedasticity check" , nrow (residual_diagnostics), sum (residual_diagnostics $ heteroscedasticity_assessment == "acceptable" ), sum (residual_diagnostics $ heteroscedasticity_assessment == "not acceptable" ), "Four conservative screen flags retained; the final visual assessment is acceptable." ) |> gt :: gt () |> gt :: fmt_integer ( columns = c ( Targets_or_rows, Acceptable_or_clear, Limitations_or_screen_flags ) ) |> gt :: cols_label ( Targets_or_rows = "Targets or rows" , Acceptable_or_clear = "Acceptable or clear" , Limitations_or_screen_flags = "Retained limitations or screen flags" ) |> prep_gt ( 9 ) Table 11: Stored final model-check assessments and retained quantitative screens. Record Targets or rows Acceptable or clear Retained limitations or screen flags Interpretation Overall target assessment 24 18 6 Final interpreted assessment across 16 domains. Integrated distribution check 24 16 8 Eight conservative screen flags retained; the final visual assessment is acceptable. Lower-level distribution screen 24 10 14 Fourteen all-threshold flags retained, including outlier-only flags. Heteroscedasticity check 24 20 4 Four conservative screen flags retained; the final visual assessment is acceptable. The retained limitations among those six targets have specific interpretations. The two near-eye last-timing slopes were close to zero and changed direction under some participant-deletion and leave-one-site-out checks, although no deletion changed a slope by the material 0.25-hour threshold. The chest longest-period/MEQ maximum-likelihood chronotype-by-site interaction fit was singular; its additive average-association fit remained estimable. The registered longest-period outcome was unavailable in the gap-timing-unaware prepared artifact at both placements and for both instruments. Fixed-effect matrices were full rank and Hessians positive definite for all stored fits. The complete model-check registry , screen-to-final assessment record , participant-influence summary , and leave-one-site-out summary preserve the values and assessment basis. No model-check flag automatically removes an observation.

title: H10: Age, measured biological sex, and personal light exposure – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Hypothesis and question The preregistered hypothesis was: “Personal light exposure metrics depend on age and gender.” Biological sex and gender were recorded as separate variables; the accepted analyses used biological sex, coded Female or Male; gender was not analysed. The confirmatory question evaluated here is whether age or measured biological sex is associated with personal light-exposure metrics. These metrics include melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance (melEDI), an illuminance weighted for melanopsin-related sensitivity. Note Answer in brief Every interval below is a 95% confidence interval (95% CI). After false-discovery-rate (FDR) adjustment, each additional decade of age at the primary near-eye sensor position was associated with a 1.31-fold brightest-10-hour mean (95% CI 1.09–1.58; FDR-adjusted p = 0.018 ), 1.27-fold time above 1,000 lx melEDI (1.11–1.45; 0.009 ), and 1.31-fold melEDI dose (1.09–1.56; 0.018 ). No near-eye Female-minus-Male contrast or near-eye predictor-by-site interaction met its separately labelled 17-metric FDR rule. Complementary chest models retained six age associations and two Female-minus-Male contrasts, but the sensor positions were not pooled and their similarity was not treated as equivalence. The directions of all 11 retained main findings persisted in the common-sample, remaining-gap, and preregistration-exclusion checks for which they were estimable.
