text: Methods and rationale

title: H10: Age, measured biological sex, and personal light exposure – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Data, outcomes, and estimands The near-eye sensor position was primary because it sampled light closer to the eyes during wear, although it did not directly measure retinal exposure. The chest sensor position provided complementary environmental evidence, not ocular exposure. A participant-day is one participant’s retained daily record on one local calendar day. The 17 registered outcomes cover daily stability and fragmentation, light level, duration, timing, exposure history, and spectrum. Depending on the outcome, the primary near-eye models used 137–141 participants and 655–816 participant-days; chest models used 152–154 participants and 732–902 participant-days. The observed age range was 18–68 years. Exact fitted samples and valid support hours are reported with every main-effect estimate below. The primary estimand was the site-adjusted common association across the observed sites. Separate interaction models allowed the age or biological-sex association to differ by study site. Age was represented as age_decade = age / 10 , so its coefficient is directly the cross-sectional association per 10-year increase. This rescaling changes only the coefficient’s unit: using age in years and rescaling the resulting coefficient and confidence limits would give the same fitted values and inferential p -values. These cross-sectional coefficients are not causal effects of ageing. Measured biological sex was treatment-coded with Male as the reference, making each contrast Female minus Male. Age and measured biological sex were fitted in separate model sets. Near-eye and chest observations were never pooled, and no equivalence margin was specified. Several outcomes were fitted on transformed scales. Their practical effects were back-transformed , meaning converted from the model scale to ratios or other outcome-scale quantities. Standardized transformed-scale effects appear only as display quantities that place differently scaled outcomes on a common visual axis; the tables retain practical-scale estimates. Metric derivation and support are documented in Preparation 04 , and construction of the model-ready datasets is documented in Preparation 06 . Daily MDER was defined as the arithmetic mean of viable one-minute melEDI/illuminance ratios on a complete 1,440-minute local wall-clock grid. A minute was viable only when both channels were finite and strictly positive, and a daily value required at least 720 viable minutes. Duplicate fall-back minutes were averaged channel-wise before the ratio was formed; absent spring-forward minutes remained missing. No time-profile weighting was used.

title: H10: Age, measured biological sex, and personal light exposure – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Models and multiplicity Participant-day outcomes used a participant random effect nested in site. This random effect represents remaining between-participant variation after the fixed predictors and study site are considered, while accounting for repeated days from the same participant. IS and IV have one row per participant and therefore used the same fixed effects without a random effect. Table 1: Registered model formulas. Model Wilkinson formula Purpose Reduced response ~ site + (1 | site:Id) Site adjustment Age response ~ site + age_decade + (1 | site:Id) Common age association Age × site response ~ site * age_decade + (1 | site:Id) Age-by-site interaction Biological sex response ~ site + biological_sex + (1 | site:Id) Common Female-minus-Male contrast Biological sex × site response ~ site * biological_sex + (1 | site:Id) Biological-sex-by-site interaction These are the exact Wilkinson formulas for participant-day outcomes. Participant-level IS and IV omit the random-intercept term. Gaussian mixed models used maximum likelihood for nested comparisons and REML for final coefficients and 95% CIs. Participant-level Gaussian models used partial F tests and t -based CIs. Tweedie/log mixed models used likelihood-ratio tests and normal-approximation CIs. Time below 10 lx melEDI before sleep used a Gaussian identity model on hours . No bootstrap, simulation, or other resampling was required. Ratios for log10-offset models are back-transformed practical effects. Multiplicity was controlled with four separate complete 17-test FDR families for each sensor position and dataset: age main effects, biological-sex main effects, age-by-site interactions, and biological-sex-by-site interactions. For time below 1 lx melEDI during sleep, four observed zeros at each sensor position exceeded the fitted Tweedie zero mass; standardized differences were 467–546. title: H10: Age, measured biological sex, and personal light exposure – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Interpretation and limitations The primary evidence supports positive age associations with selected near-eye measures of brighter exposure and accumulated melEDI. It does not support a near-eye Female-minus-Male contrast after FDR adjustment, nor does it support an FDR-retained near-eye age-by-site or biological-sex-by-site interaction. Complementary chest results broaden the age pattern and identify two Female-minus-Male contrasts, but sensor-position-specific measurement context prevents treating these results as pooled evidence or as proof that sensor positions are equivalent. The coefficients describe cross-sectional associations within the observed age range and sites; they are not causal effects of ageing or biological sex. Biological sex was the construct actually recorded, and the analysis provides no inference about gender identity. Site adjustment addresses measured site differences in the specified model but cannot remove all demographic, behavioural, seasonal, occupational, or environmental confounding. Residual and leave-one-site-out findings qualify several estimates even though no model failed the explicit acceptability rule. The strongest retained main findings were directionally robust across the available sensitivity analyses, but three changed adjusted-support status under at least one stricter common-sample comparison. The model-ready input layer and current light-metric values, including the gap-timing-unaware dataset, were independently verified; complete independent reconstruction of the exact current state-support classification remains open . That provenance qualification is not evidence that the stored values are incorrect.

text: Preregistration deviations DEV-003 is a current qualification: retained samples include documented participants outside the preregistered age or employment criteria, and exclusion-sensitivity coverage is not uniform across all affected hypotheses. The H10 sensitivity above does not resolve that broader qualification. DEV-040 records that all planned age-by-site and biological-sex-by-site interactions are fitted, tested, and reported, with non-estimable branches kept visible. DEV-041 records four separate complete 17-metric FDR families: age main effects, biological-sex main effects, age-by-site interactions, and biological-sex-by-site interactions.

Model estimates and intervals, model checks, influence results, sensitivity analyses, figures, and source data are read from stored H10 outputs. This page does not fit or compare models, calculate predictions, repeat influence checks, bootstrap, resample, or simulate data. The preregistered hypothesis was: Personal light exposure metrics depend on age and gender. Biological sex and gender were recorded as separate variables. The accepted analyses used biological sex, coded Female or Male; gender was not analysed. Age associations were estimated per 10-year increase and describe cross-sectional associations, not causal effects of ageing. The primary estimands were the site-adjusted common age association and Female-minus-Male association. Separate age-by-site and biological-sex-by-site interactions allowed those associations to differ by study site. The primary near-eye sensor position sampled light closer to the eyes during wear, although it did not directly measure retinal exposure. The complementary chest sensor position measured light at the chest, not ocular exposure. The 17 responses include melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance (melEDI), an illuminance weighted for melanopsin-related sensitivity. A participant-day is one participant’s retained daily record on one local calendar day. Every reported interval is a 95% confidence interval (95% CI). Four separate complete 17-test families use false-discovery-rate (FDR) adjustment: age main effects, biological-sex main effects, age-by-site interactions, and biological-sex-by-site interactions. Metric derivation and support are documented in Preparation 04 , and model-ready dataset construction is documented in Preparation 06 . The H10 results report presents the scientific findings and its linked registration-record summary .

title: H10 analysis preparation and provenance – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Verified inputs and current qualification The analysis used the current Preparation 06 model-ready layer. Its base objects contained 816 near-eye and 902 chest participant-days before metric-specific availability was applied. The model-ready layer, current MDER values, and L10 numerical-zero normalization were independently verified. The L10 normalization changed exactly eight primary L10 values from numerical noise to exact zero without changing a sample, a non-L10 scientific value, or an inferential decision. The corrected gap-timing-unaware chest day with no viable momentary ratio is recorded as missing, and every finite gap MDER value is strictly positive. The remaining qualification is explicit: complete independent reconstruction of the exact current state-support classification remains open . This qualification is not evidence that the stored values are incorrect.

text: Demographic construct and site support Age and biological sex were joined as participant-level variables and were complete in every fitted frame. Biological sex had exactly the levels Male and Female. Male was the reference, so the reported coefficient is Female minus Male. Site was explicitly sum-coded. title: H10 analysis preparation and provenance – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Exact Wilkinson formulae For participant-day outcomes, the random effect (1 | site:Id) accounts for repeated days within participant and represents remaining between-participant variation after the fixed predictors and study site are considered. IS and IV have one row per participant, so an ordinary site-adjusted linear model avoids a non-identifiable one-observation random effect. The exact evaluated formulae stored with the model records are: Show the R code used for this display model_labels <- c ( M0 = "Site-only reference" , M_age = "Site-adjusted age association" , M_age_site = "Age-by-site interaction" , M_sex = "Site-adjusted Female-minus-Male association" , M_sex_site = "Biological-sex-by-site interaction" ) model_manifest |> filter (.data $ fit_role == "maximum_likelihood_comparison" ) |> distinct (.data $ analysis_unit, .data $ model_name, .data $ formula) |> mutate ( ` Analysis unit ` = if_else ( .data $ analysis_unit == "participant" , "Participant" , "Participant-day" ), Model = unname (model_labels[.data $ model_name]) ) |> arrange (.data $ ` Analysis unit ` , match (.data $ model_name, names (model_labels))) |> select ( "Analysis unit" , "Model" , Formula = "formula" ) |> prep_gt ( font_size = 9 ) Table 6: Exact evaluated Wilkinson formulae. Analysis unit Model Formula Participant Site-only reference response ~ site Participant Site-adjusted age association response ~ site + age_decade Participant Age-by-site interaction response ~ site * age_decade Participant Site-adjusted Female-minus-Male association response ~ site + biological_sex Participant Biological-sex-by-site interaction response ~ site * biological_sex Participant-day Site-only reference response ~ site + (1 | site:Id) Participant-day Site-adjusted age association response ~ site + age_decade + (1 | site:Id) Participant-day Age-by-site interaction response ~ site * age_decade + (1 | site:Id) Participant-day Site-adjusted Female-minus-Male association response ~ site + biological_sex + (1 | site:Id) Participant-day Biological-sex-by-site interaction response ~ site * biological_sex + (1 | site:Id) Age was represented as age_decade = age / 10 ; this changes the coefficient’s unit but not fitted values or test statistics. Its coefficient is the cross-sectional association per 10-year increase, not a causal ageing effect. Site used sum contrasts. Biological sex used Male then Female treatment coding. The additive coefficient was the site-adjusted common association. An interaction comparison asked separately whether the association varied among sites. Where an interaction summary uses a site-average estimate , it is an average across the represented sites that gives each site equal weight.

title: H10 analysis preparation and provenance – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Engines, estimation, and confidence intervals Gaussian participant-day comparisons were fitted by maximum likelihood and their final coefficients by REML. Gaussian participant-level models used ordinary least squares. Tweedie/log models used maximum likelihood. The model record contains 612 fits: five comparison fits and four final fits for each of 68 frames. Show the R code used for this display model_manifest |> count ( .data $ analysis_unit, .data $ response_family, .data $ engine, .data $ fit_role, name = "Fits" ) |> transmute ( ` Analysis unit ` = str_replace_all (.data $ analysis_unit, "_" , "-" ), ` Response family ` = recode ( .data $ response_family, gaussian = "Gaussian" , tweedie_log = "Tweedie, log link" ), Engine = .data $ engine, ` Estimation role ` = recode ( .data $ fit_role, maximum_likelihood_comparison = "Maximum-likelihood comparison" , REML_final_estimation = "REML final estimation" , final_estimation_same_as_ML = "Final estimate from maximum likelihood" ), Fits = .data $ Fits ) |> arrange (.data $ ` Analysis unit ` , .data $ ` Response family ` , .data $ ` Estimation role ` ) |> prep_gt ( font_size = 9 ) Table 7: Model engines and estimation roles. Analysis unit Response family Engine Estimation role Fits participant Gaussian lm Final estimate from maximum likelihood 32 participant Gaussian lm Maximum-likelihood comparison 40 participant-day Gaussian lmerMod Maximum-likelihood comparison 240 participant-day Gaussian lmerMod REML final estimation 192 participant-day Tweedie, log link glmmTMB Final estimate from maximum likelihood 48 participant-day Tweedie, log link glmmTMB Maximum-likelihood comparison 60 Every reported coefficient has a model-based 95% CI. Ordinary linear-model coefficients use a residual-degree-of-freedom t interval; mixed-model and Tweedie coefficients use the fixed-effect covariance matrix with a normal critical value. Logit effects are odds ratios, base-10 transformed Gaussian effects are ratios, Tweedie/log effects are ratios, and identity-scale effects are differences. Clock-time differences are reported in minutes. Back-transformed effects have been converted from the model scale to these practical ratios or differences.

title: H10 analysis preparation and provenance – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Interaction tests and multiplicity Four separate complete 17-metric FDR families were evaluated for each dataset and sensor position. Age main effects, biological-sex main effects, age-by-site interactions, and biological-sex-by-site interactions were never combined into one family. Show the R code used for this display comparison_labels <- c ( "AGE-MAIN" = "Age main association" , "SEX-MAIN" = "Biological-sex main association" , "AGE-SITE" = "Age-by-site interaction" , "SEX-SITE" = "Biological-sex-by-site interaction" ) family_audit |> filter (.data $ data_scenario == "primary" ) |> transmute ( Placement = if_else ( .data $ placement == "glasses" , "Near eye (primary)" , "Chest (complementary)" ), Family = unname (comparison_labels[.data $ comparison_id]), ` Planned tests ` = .data $ planned_n, ` Observed raw p-values ` = .data $ observed_raw_p, ` Retained results ` = .data $ adjusted_significant_n, ` Complete family ` = if_else ( .data $ complete_17_member_family, "Yes" , "No" ), ` Independent FDR check ` = if_else ( .data $ independent_recalculation_matches, "PASS" , "FAIL" ) ) |> arrange (.data $ Placement, match (.data $ Family, unname (comparison_labels))) |> prep_gt ( note = paste0 ( "Significance was decided from numeric adjusted p-values before " , "formatting. Every family used FDR adjustment with planned n = 17." ) ) Table 8: Primary-dataset multiplicity families. Placement Family Planned tests Observed raw p-values Retained results Complete family Independent FDR check Chest (complementary) Age main association 17 17 6 Yes PASS Chest (complementary) Biological-sex main association 17 17 2 Yes PASS Chest (complementary) Age-by-site interaction 17 17 2 Yes PASS Chest (complementary) Biological-sex-by-site interaction 17 17 0 Yes PASS Near eye (primary) Age main association 17 17 3 Yes PASS Near eye (primary) Biological-sex main association 17 17 0 Yes PASS Near eye (primary) Age-by-site interaction 17 17 0 Yes PASS Near eye (primary) Biological-sex-by-site interaction 17 17 0 Yes PASS Significance was decided from numeric adjusted p-values before formatting. Every family used FDR adjustment with planned n = 17. The stored primary package contains 136 main-effect estimates and 272 model comparisons. Eleven main associations and two complementary-chest age-by-site interactions met their separately labelled adjusted rules. Site-specific interaction components were stored with 95% CIs as descriptive estimates, not as a new set of site-level significance tests.

title: H10 analysis preparation and provenance – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Model checks, influence, and limitations All 612 fits converged, had positive-definite Hessians and full-rank fixed effects, were non-singular, and emitted no fit error. Model checks were interpreted for 68 primary metric-sensor-position-association targets: 25 were acceptable and 43 acceptable with specified limitations; none was classified not acceptable. Show the R code used for this display diagnostic_summary <- tibble :: tribble ( ~ Domain, ~ Stored_evidence, ~ Assessment, "Fit and rank" , sprintf ( "%d fits" , nrow (model_manifest)), "All converged; positive-definite Hessians; full-rank fixed effects; no singular fit or fit error." , "Residual and distributional checks" , sprintf ( "%d primary targets" , nrow (diagnostic_assessment)), "Residual spread, Q–Q correlation, fitted-response bounds, dispersion, and zero-mass evidence were interpreted jointly." , "Temporal dependence" , sprintf ( "%s consecutive-day residual pairs" , format_count ( sum (diagnostic_assessment $ consecutive_day_pairs, na.rm = TRUE ))), sprintf ( "All 60 participant-day checks passed the descriptive threshold; maximum absolute correlation %.3f." , max ( abs (diagnostic_assessment $ pooled_consecutive_day_residual_correlation), na.rm = TRUE )), "Participant deletion" , sprintf ( "%d target summaries" , nrow (participant_influence)), sprintf ( "Every check passed; maximum change %.3f full-fit standard errors." , max (participant_influence $ change_in_full_standard_errors, na.rm = TRUE )), "Leave one site out" , sprintf ( "%d target summaries" , nrow (leave_one_site_summary)), sprintf ( "No failed refit; maximum change %.2f full-fit standard errors." , max (leave_one_site_summary $ max_change_in_full_standard_errors, na.rm = TRUE )), "Final classification" , "25 acceptable; 43 acceptable with specified limitations" , "No primary target was classified not acceptable." ) diagnostic_summary |> prep_gt ( font_size = 9 ) Table 9: Stored model-check and influence evidence. Domain Stored_evidence Assessment Fit and rank 612 fits All converged; positive-definite Hessians; full-rank fixed effects; no singular fit or fit error. Residual and distributional checks 68 primary targets Residual spread, Q–Q correlation, fitted-response bounds, dispersion, and zero-mass evidence were interpreted jointly. Temporal dependence 37,576 consecutive-day residual pairs All 60 participant-day checks passed the descriptive threshold; maximum absolute correlation 0.239. Participant deletion 68 target summaries Every check passed; maximum change 0.319 full-fit standard errors. Leave one site out 68 target summaries No failed refit; maximum change 1.72 full-fit standard errors. Final classification 25 acceptable; 43 acceptable with specified limitations No primary target was classified not acceptable. The most recurrent qualifications were residual-spread or Q–Q flags for selected right-skewed or timing responses, plus a zero-mass mismatch for sleep- environment time below 1 lx melEDI. Four observed zeros at each sensor position remained in those fitted Tweedie models. These issues were retained in the interpretation rather than used to select an unregistered replacement model. Complete numerical model-check results are available in the assessment file , participant-deletion , and leave-one-site-out files. The results report also displays residual-versus-fitted and descriptive normal Q-Q plots for all 11 multiplicity-retained main-association models. A 68-page appendix provides the same core plots for all 68 primary models, with an exact page and assessment index and complete plot data . These displays are constructed from the stored fitted values, Pearson residuals, and Q-Q points already produced by the analysis; no model is refitted and no assessment is recalculated.

title: H10 analysis preparation and provenance – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Sensitivity analyses Each sensitivity analysis changed one declared feature while retaining the H10 estimand and model implementation. The gap-timing-unaware dataset applies the same general coverage rules as the primary dataset but does not use the timing of remaining missing observations for metric-specific adjustment. The sensitivity analyses were not used to replace the primary conclusion. The primary MDER frames contained 702 near-eye participant-days from 137 participants and 732 chest participant-days from 152 participants. The gap-timing-unaware MDER frames contained 687 near-eye participant-days from 137 participants and 723 chest participant-days from 152 participants. The paired gap MDER branch used 478 participant-days from 107 participants at each sensor position, and the exact primary-versus-gap common samples used 687 near-eye and 723 chest participant-days. Every finite MDER value was strictly positive; the chest day with no viable momentary ratio was reason-coded missing.

title: H10 analysis preparation and provenance – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Linked preregistration deviations DEV-003 is a current qualification: retained samples include documented participants outside the preregistered age or employment criteria, and exclusion-sensitivity coverage is not uniform across all affected hypotheses. The H10 exclusion sensitivity does not resolve that broader qualification. DEV-040 records that all planned age-by-site and biological-sex-by-site interactions are fitted, tested, and reported, with non-estimable branches kept visible. DEV-041 records four separate complete 17-metric FDR families: age main effects, biological-sex main effects, age-by-site interactions, and biological-sex-by-site interactions. The H10 results deviation section gives the reciprocal reader summary.

title: H11: Biological sex and daily personal light-exposure patterns – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: H11: Biological sex and daily personal light-exposure patterns Sex-specific 24-hour melanopic light-exposure curves at near-eye and chest level Last modified: August 12, 2026

title: H11: Biological sex and daily personal light-exposure patterns – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Question The preregistered hypothesis was: “H11: Diurnal exposure patterns differ by sex.” The recorded predictor is biological sex , coded Female or Male. Gender identity is a distinct construct and was not analysed. The analytical question is whether the fitted 24-hour personal melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance (melEDI) profile differs between participants recorded as Female and Male after accounting for site-specific temporal patterns, repeated observations within participants and days, and short-lag residual dependence. Tip Answer in brief After false-discovery-rate (FDR) adjustment, the primary near-eye Female-minus-Male curve differed globally (adjusted p = 0.028 ), and the complementary chest curve also differed globally (adjusted p = 0.029 ). The secondary level/shape analysis could not cleanly assign either globally supported curve to an independently resolved level or shape component; this does not overturn the global results. In the exploratory activity-complete sample, near eye was already unsupported before activity adjustment (raw p = 0.160) and remained unsupported after it (raw p = 0.364). At chest, the corresponding raw p -value changed from 0.025 to 0.050. This sensitivity is compatible with attenuation but cannot identify activity as a mechanism. Model checks classified all accepted fits as acceptable with specified limitations.

title: H11: Biological sex and daily personal light-exposure patterns – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: What was analysed The near-eye sensor position is primary because it measures the light field closer to the eyes. The chest sensor position is analysed separately as complementary evidence and is not a measure of ocular exposure. The placements are neither pooled nor treated as independent replicates. The response is the 30-minute arithmetic mean melEDI, modelled as log10(melEDI + 0.1) . The estimand is the complete fitted Female-minus-Male 24-hour curve at equal clock-time weighting. Its site-average fitted mean averages across included sites and gives each site equal weight. The participant is the independent unit for robust inference. A participant-day is one participant’s included observations on one local calendar day. Table 1: Exact fitted samples for the primary near-eye and complementary chest analyses. Role Participants Female / Male participants Participant-days 30-minute observations Sites Near eye Primary 141 79 / 62 816 37,756 9 Chest Complementary 154 86 / 68 902 41,842 8 The primary near-eye model contains 141 participants (79 Female, 62 Male), 816 participant-days, 37,756 30-minute observations, and all nine sites. The chest model contains 154 participants (86 Female, 68 Male), 902 participant-days, 41,842 observations, and eight sites. These are the accepted temporal-model samples; no extra H11-specific row deletion was applied. Note Key terms Site-average fitted mean: the fitted mean averaged across included sites, with each site given equal weight. Complete-curve test: one joint test of the time-constant and time-varying Female-minus-Male contributions across the whole 24-hour curve. Pointwise 95% confidence interval (95% CI): uncertainty for one displayed clock bin; it is not a simultaneous band across the full day. Shifted-value ratio: both fitted melEDI values are shifted by the model’s 0.1-lx offset before the Female-to-Male ratio is calculated. AR(1): a representation of autocorrelation in which residual similarity is stronger for measurements closer together in time. Symlog: a display scale that is linear from 0 to 1 lx and base-10 logarithmic above 1 lx, with labels retained in original units.

title: H11: Biological sex and daily personal light-exposure patterns – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Model and inference The nonlinear generalized additive model (GAM) allows the daily melEDI pattern to vary smoothly and nonlinearly over clock time. Its cyclic common daily curve and cyclic Female-specific deviation join smoothly across midnight. The model also includes site-specific temporal deviations, participant-specific time curves, and participant-day random effects. The latter two represent remaining repeated-measure variation after the shared time, biological-sex, and site structure is considered. Autocorrelation is residual similarity between measurements close together in time. An AR(1) structure represents this dependence as stronger at shorter lags. Sequence starts prevent that correlation from crossing participant-day or gap boundaries. The detailed estimation and robust-covariance specification is documented in the preparation and provenance companion. The following evaluated R cell reads and prints the exact Wilkinson formula supplied to every accepted H11 full model. Here, response is the transformed melEDI outcome and Male is the reference level. accepted_h11_formula <- stats :: as.formula (formula_registry $ formula[[ 1 L]]) accepted_h11_formula response ~ sex + s(time_hour, bs = "cc", k = 12) + s(time_hour, by = sex_smooth, bs = "cc", k = 12) + s(time_hour, site, bs = "sz", k = 12) + s(time_hour, participant, bs = "fs", k = 10) + s(participant_day, bs = "re") The complete-curve, or global, test jointly evaluates the time-constant and time-varying contributions to the 48-bin Female-minus-Male curve. It produces one decision per placement and dataset. FDR adjustment is applied within separately labelled test families. Each global family has one test. The planned level and shape attribution tests form a separate two-test FDR family within each placement. Those secondary tests do not repeat the global test, and failure to resolve either component does not invalidate a supported global curve. All curve and contrast intervals are participant-cluster-robust pointwise 95% CIs. Each applies to one displayed clock bin and does not support a simultaneous significant-period claim. Table 2: Complete-curve tests for the primary near-eye and complementary chest analyses. Role Test F statistic Numerator df Denominator df Raw p FDR-adjusted p Support Near eye Primary Complete Female-minus-Male 24-hour curve 20.946 9.692 131 0.028 0.028 Supported Chest Complementary Complete Female-minus-Male 24-hour curve 4.876 1.003 152 0.029 0.029 Supported Primary near-eye fitted sample: 141 participants, 816 participant-days, 37,756 30-minute observations, and 9 sites. Complementary chest fitted sample: 154 participants, 902 participant-days, 41,842 30-minute observations, and 8 sites. Each row is one joint complete-curve test. Raw p is bold at raw p < 0.050; FDR-adjusted p is bold independently at adjusted p < 0.050. Each labelled global family contains one test, so the stored raw and adjusted values coincide. Both complete curves were supported. For near eye, raw p and FDR-adjusted p were 0.028 . For chest, raw p and FDR-adjusted p were 0.029 . Within each one-test global family, the stored raw and adjusted values are identical.

Ribbons and contrast intervals are participant-cluster-robust pointwise 95% confidence intervals, not simultaneous bands. The melEDI panel uses the approved symlog scale, linear from 0 to 1 lx and base-10 logarithmic above 1 lx, with labels in original units. The fitted sample contains 141 participants, 816 participant-days, 37,756 30-minute observations, and nine sites. title: H11: Biological sex and daily personal light-exposure patterns – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
section: Can the global results be separated into level and shape?
text: Can the global results be separated into level and shape? These secondary attribution tests are subordinate to the complete-curve tests in Table 2 . They ask whether each globally supported curve can be assigned cleanly to an independently supported level or shape component.

title: H11: Biological sex and daily personal light-exposure patterns – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Primary near eye Table 5: Primary near-eye level and shape attribution. F statistic Numerator df Raw p FDR-adjusted p Conclusion Near eye Level 3.213 1.000 0.075 0.075 Not supported Shape 17.896 8.692 0.043 0.075 Not supported Within each placement and dataset, level and shape form a two-test false-discovery-rate family. Raw and adjusted p-values are labelled and bolded independently at their respective p < 0.050 rules. These secondary tests ask whether the globally tested curve can be resolved into an independently supported level or shape component; they do not retest or invalidate the separate global curve result. The secondary attribution did not cleanly resolve the globally supported curve into an independently supported level or shape component. The shape component had raw p = 0.043 but FDR-adjusted p = 0.075; the level component had raw and adjusted p = 0.075. The global result is not formed by adding or combining these two p -values. Evidence can be distributed across correlated level and shape directions, so this result expresses uncertainty about attribution and does not make the global result invalid.

text: Complementary chest Table 6: Complementary chest level and shape attribution. F statistic Numerator df Raw p FDR-adjusted p Conclusion Chest Level 4.877 1.000 0.029 0.057 Not supported Shape 0.000 0.003 0.986 0.986 Not supported Within each placement and dataset, level and shape form a two-test false-discovery-rate family. Raw and adjusted p-values are labelled and bolded independently at their respective p < 0.050 rules. These secondary tests ask whether the globally tested curve can be resolved into an independently supported level or shape component; they do not retest or invalidate the separate global curve result. The chest global result is visually level-like, but the secondary attribution did not resolve that result independently to the level term: its raw p = 0.029 and FDR-adjusted p = 0.057. The shape component had raw and adjusted p = 0.986. This limits component attribution and does not overturn the separately supported complete-curve result.

title: H11: Biological sex and daily personal light-exposure patterns – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
section: Why there is no direct placement identity plot
text: Why there is no direct placement identity plot The all-available near-eye and chest models use different samples, so plotting their estimates against one another would confound placement with sample composition. A stored common frame contains 112 participants, 643 participant- days, 29,786 matched observations, and eight sites, but no accepted H11 model was fitted to that frame and no scalar temporal estimand was predeclared. Therefore a matched identity scatterplot is not applicable. The separate near-eye and chest curves above are the closest valid comparison; they do not test placement differences or establish equivalence.

title: H11: Biological sex and daily personal light-exposure patterns – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Exploratory activity-context sensitivity The accepted global test remains unadjusted for activity. An exploratory sensitivity asked whether the estimated Female-minus-Male curve changed after adding the recorded hourly activity context. To separate adjustment from sample selection, the accepted H11 model was first refitted without activity on the exact activity-complete sample and then refitted with activity on those same observations. Diary hours were eligible only when exactly one activity was selected. Hours with multiple selections, no selection, all missing responses, or only an unspecified “other” activity were excluded rather than duplicated across categories. The retained contexts were home (reference), sleep, road or vehicle, indoor work, and outdoor activity. A 30-minute exposure observation was attached only when it lay wholly within one unique diary hour. This restriction produced the following exact samples. They converged without serious fitting warnings; the cyclic sex curves close at midnight; site deviations satisfy their sum-to-zero constraint; and no severe basis- dimension flag was found. The accepted AR structure reduced boundary-aware lag-1 residual correlation from approximately 0.60–0.62 before adjustment to 0.070–0.083 in the final residuals. Panel A shows stored final standardized-residual quantiles overall and by recorded biological sex: thin lines span the 1st–99th percentiles, medium lines the 5th–95th percentiles, thick lines the interquartile range, and points the median. Residual-distribution diagnostic source data Together, the residual figures show the main continuous diagnostic outcomes: the accepted AR(1) structure removes most short-lag dependence, while the final residuals remain centered near zero but retain heavy tails and fitted-value-dependent spread. Convergence, cyclic closure, the site constraint, and basis-dimension flags remain in the diagnostic table because they are pass/fail or count outcomes rather than quantities that benefit from a separate plot. No single participant dominates the robust covariance: the largest participant contribution is 2.8–3.0% near eye and 7.5–7.6% at chest. The coefficient-held-fixed delete-one-participant covariance check retains the global decision for every participant. Exact zeros, heavy tails, heteroscedasticity, and concurvity remain under the Gaussian log-scale mean model. The registered hourly geometric-mean outcome remains the documented preregistered specification but is outside the accepted H11 analysis rather than an outstanding sensitivity. A fitted common-placement sample, an all-zero-inclusive preparation, and alternative temporal model forms remain unresolved. title: H11: Biological sex and daily personal light-exposure patterns – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Interpretation These data support a biological-sex difference in the complete fitted daily melEDI profile at near-eye level, with complementary support at chest level. Near-eye pointwise estimates indicate the largest relative separation around the morning, whereas the chest contrast is nearly time-constant. However, the planned component analysis cannot attribute the supported joint result specifically to a level or shape component after multiplicity adjustment. That attribution limitation does not weaken the definition or validity of the separate global curve test. Activity adjustment did not yield a supported adjusted global curve on the activity-complete sample at either placement. For near eye, however, the same-sample unadjusted curve was already unsupported, so the change cannot be assigned to activity. For chest, the curve magnitude changed modestly and the raw p -value moved just above 0.050. Neither pattern establishes mediation or a causal activity pathway. The effect-size summaries are modest on the fitted model scale, and all clock- specific confidence intervals are pointwise. The result is therefore evidence for an overall structured association, not proof of a significant clock period, not an equivalence or placement-difference analysis, and not evidence that biological sex causally determines light exposure. Differences may reflect behavioural, occupational, environmental, or other correlated factors that this observational model does not identify.

title: H11 analysis preparation and provenance – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Purpose This page explains how the verified H02 temporal frames and recorded biological sex were turned into the inference presented in the H11 results report . H11 asks whether the 24-hour pattern of personal melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance (melEDI) differs by the biological-sex variable recorded in the study. Biological sex and gender identity are distinct constructs; gender identity was not analysed. The near-eye sensor position is primary. The chest sensor position provides complementary evidence and is not a measure of ocular exposure. This placement change is recorded in DEV-001 . The reported estimand is the complete Female-minus-Male fitted curve across 48 half-hour clock bins, averaged equally across included sites and conditional on the fitted temporal, participant, participant-day, site, and autocorrelation structure. A site-average fitted mean averages across included sites and gives each site equal weight. The participant is the independent unit for robust inference. A participant-day is one participant’s included observations on one local calendar day; model rows are 30-minute observations nested within participant-days and participants. The accepted preregistration differences are consolidated in the H11 preregistration-deviations section .

title: H11 analysis preparation and provenance – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Inherited time structure H11 inherits the finalized temporal architecture documented in the H02 analysis preparation and provenance rather than selecting a new one. Local wall-clock time is represented by 48 half-hour midpoints from 00:15 to 23:45. The smooth is cyclic, meaning that it joins smoothly across midnight. Site-specific time patterns sum to zero, participant-specific time curves represent remaining within-participant variation, and participant-day random effects represent remaining variation within local calendar days. The hierarchy and site structure are recorded in DEV-044 and DEV-045 . Autocorrelation sequences are based on true elapsed instants. A sequence restarts at participant-day boundaries, elapsed-time discontinuities, and non-one-to-one wall-clock outcomes, including daylight-saving-time ambiguity. The accepted frames therefore do not infer continuity merely because two rows have adjacent clock labels. title: H11 analysis preparation and provenance – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: 2. Nonlinear GAM construction A nonlinear generalized additive model (GAM) allows the daily melEDI pattern to vary smoothly and nonlinearly over clock time. Cyclic smooths join smoothly across midnight. Participant-specific time curves and participant-day random effects represent remaining repeated-measure variation after the shared time, biological-sex, and site structure is considered. Autocorrelation is residual similarity between observations close together in time; an AR(1) structure represents this similarity as stronger at shorter lags.

title: H11 analysis preparation and provenance – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Exact Wilkinson formulas The following are the exact formulas supplied to the accepted model fits. The cells are displayed for auditability and are not executed on this page. Show the R code used for this display M_pattern <- response ~ sex + s (time_hour, bs = "cc" , k = 12 ) + s (time_hour, by = sex_smooth, bs = "cc" , k = 12 ) + s (time_hour, site, bs = "sz" , k = 12 ) + s (time_hour, participant, bs = "fs" , k = 10 ) + s (participant_day, bs = "re" ) Show the R code used for this display M_0 <- response ~ s (time_hour, bs = "cc" , k = 12 ) + s (time_hour, site, bs = "sz" , k = 12 ) + s (time_hour, participant, bs = "fs" , k = 10 ) + s (participant_day, bs = "re" ) Show the R code used for this display M_activity <- response ~ sex + activity + s (time_hour, bs = "cc" , k = 12 ) + s (time_hour, by = sex_smooth, bs = "cc" , k = 12 ) + s (time_hour, by = activity_smooth, bs = "cc" , k = 12 , id = 2 ) + s (time_hour, site, bs = "sz" , k = 12 ) + s (time_hour, participant, bs = "fs" , k = 10 ) + s (participant_day, bs = "re" ) Show the R code used for this display M_activity_0 <- response ~ activity + s (time_hour, bs = "cc" , k = 12 ) + s (time_hour, by = activity_smooth, bs = "cc" , k = 12 , id = 2 ) + s (time_hour, site, bs = "sz" , k = 12 ) + s (time_hour, participant, bs = "fs" , k = 10 ) + s (participant_day, bs = "re" ) The sex factor uses Male as the treatment-reference level. The ordered sex_smooth factor identifies the cyclic Female-minus-Male deviation. The main cyclic smooth is the Male reference curve; the sex-deviation smooth adds the Female shape difference. Site deviations use the sum-to-zero basis, participant curves use factor smooths, and participant-day random intercepts account for repeated observations within days. In the activity model, Home is the treatment reference and the ordered activity deviation smooths share one smoothing parameter ( id = 2 ). The biological-sex/time specification is recorded in DEV-043 , and the site and participant structure is recorded in DEV-044 and DEV-045 .

text: 3. Estimand, uncertainty, and multiplicity

title: H11 analysis preparation and provenance – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Complete-curve inference The complete-curve, or global, test is one joint test of the time-constant and time-varying Female-minus-Male contributions across the whole 48-bin, 24-hour curve within each placement and dataset. Inference uses participant-summed, AR-whitened scores; a participant-cluster CR1 covariance; the smoothing-bias term V_p-V_e ; and a finite-cluster, fractional-rank F reference. A pointwise 95% confidence interval (95% CI) applies to one displayed clock bin. It is not a simultaneous band across the full day. All displayed curve, contrast, and scalar intervals are pointwise 95% CIs. The primary near-eye global raw p-value is 0.028 and the complementary chest raw p-value is 0.029. Each is the sole member of its explicitly labelled global family, so its stored adjusted value is numerically identical. FDR adjustment is applied within separately labelled families. This complete-curve inference and multiplicity specification is recorded in DEV-048 . section: What the two-component decomposition can and cannot say
text: What the two-component decomposition can and cannot say The complete-curve result is the overall test. A separate, secondary decomposition asks whether that curve difference can be attributed cleanly to (1) a constant parametric level component or (2) a cyclic shape component. Those two attribution tests form a two-test FDR family within each placement and dataset. No component remains supported after that two-test adjustment. This does not invalidate or reverse the significant global curve result. It means only that the evidence cannot cleanly separate the overall curve association into an independent “level” contribution and an independent “shape” contribution after accounting for the two attribution attempts. The two components are parameterization-dependent parts of one fitted curve and are not a second omnibus test of whether the full curve differs. text: Conditional effect-size branch The predeclared effect-size branch opens only when the placement-specific raw global test has p<0.050 . It opened for both primary placements. The reported curve-variation estimator is the mean, across 48 clock bins, of the sample variance across the two equally weighted fitted biological-sex curves. It is a conditional descriptive magnitude on the squared model-prediction scale, not variance explained. Its 95% interval uses the accepted participant-cluster robust covariance and first-order delta method. section: 4. Model checks, residual dependence, and influence
text: 4. Model checks, residual dependence, and influence The model checks (model diagnostics) covered convergence and warnings, cyclic closure at midnight, site sum-to-zero constraints, basis dimensions, residual distributions, boundary-aware residual autocorrelation, formal concurvity, robust covariance behaviour, participant influence, and agreement between the curve-space and coefficient-block formulations of the global test. Show the R code used for this display diagnostics |> transmute ( Dataset = .data $ dataset_label, Placement = .data $ placement_label, Assessment = .data $ classification, Converged = .data $ converged, ` Cyclic closure ` = .data $ cyclic_sex_curves_close_at_midnight, ` Site constraint ` = .data $ site_sum_to_zero_verified, ` Final lag-1 residual correlation ` = .data $ final_boundary_aware_lag1_correlation, ` Severe basis flags ` = .data $ severe_k_check_flags ) |> gt :: gt ( groupname_col = "Dataset" ) |> gt :: fmt_number ( columns = "Final lag-1 residual correlation" , decimals = 3 ) |> gt :: fmt_integer ( columns = "Severe basis flags" ) |> prep_gt ( font_size = 11 ) Table 12: Overall diagnostic assessment for primary and gap-timing-unaware fits Placement Assessment Converged Cyclic closure Site constraint Final lag-1 residual correlation Severe basis flags Primary dataset Near eye acceptable with specified limitations TRUE TRUE TRUE 0.083 0 Chest acceptable with specified limitations TRUE TRUE TRUE 0.070 0 Gap-timing-unaware dataset Near eye acceptable with specified limitations TRUE TRUE TRUE 0.082 0 Chest acceptable with specified limitations TRUE TRUE TRUE 0.071 0 All four models were assessed as acceptable with specified limitations . They converged without serious warnings, closed cyclically at midnight, preserved the inherited site constraint, had no severe basis-dimension flags, and reduced boundary-aware lag-1 residual correlation to 0.070–0.083. The remaining limitations are the Gaussian log-scale mean assumption, exact-zero mass, heavy residual tails, heteroscedasticity, and concurvity inherited from the H02 temporal analysis. These caution against interpreting the curves as a complete generative account of melEDI, but they did not trigger the prespecified unacceptable-model criteria. Show the R code used for this display robust_diagnostics |> transmute ( Dataset = .data $ dataset_label, Placement = .data $ placement_label, Participants = .data $ participants, ` Maximum cluster score share ` = .data $ maximum_participant_unscaled_meat_share, ` Effective clusters ` = .data $ effective_participants_unscaled_meat_trace, ` Delete-one p minimum ` = format_p (.data $ delete_one_participant_p_minimum), ` Delete-one p median ` = format_p (.data $ delete_one_participant_p_median), ` Delete-one p maximum ` = format_p (.data $ delete_one_participant_p_maximum), ` Delete-one results below 0.050 ` = .data $ delete_one_participant_below_0_05 ) |> gt :: gt ( groupname_col = "Dataset" ) |> gt :: fmt_integer ( columns = c ( "Participants" , "Delete-one results below 0.050" )) |> gt :: fmt_number ( columns = c ( "Maximum cluster score share" , "Effective clusters" ), decimals = 3 ) |> prep_gt ( font_size = 11 ) |> gt :: tab_source_note ( gt :: md ( "The displayed delete-one p-values are raw global-test values; no new multiplicity family is created by this influence screen." ) ) Table 13: Participant-cluster robust covariance and delete-one-participant stability Placement Participants Maximum cluster score share Effective clusters Delete-one p minimum Delete-one p median Delete-one p maximum Delete-one results below 0.050 Primary dataset Near eye 141 0.027 87.045 0.023 0.027 0.029 141 Chest 154 0.075 42.905 0.029 0.029 0.029 154 Gap-timing-unaware dataset Near eye 141 0.030 86.704 0.022 0.025 0.027 141 Chest 154 0.076 35.785 0.037 0.037 0.037 154 The displayed delete-one p-values are raw global-test values; no new multiplicity family is created by this influence screen. Every delete-one-participant primary and sensitivity result remained below 0.050. Maximum participant score contribution ranged from 2.7% to 7.6%, while the effective number of contributing clusters was smaller than the nominal participant count, especially for chest. The robust covariance therefore materially protects inference from within-participant dependence, but the chest result should still be read as complementary. Results remain conditional on the observed sites, and the site count is too small for broad site-population generalisation. Leave-one-site-out refits have not been completed, so site influence beyond the recorded checks remains an explicit unresolved limitation.

title: H11 analysis preparation and provenance – Nature Health analysis and manuscript
text: Gap timing The gap-timing-unaware dataset still passed the general requirement for at least 50% valid data per hour and at least 80% valid data per participant-day. “Gap-timing-unaware” means that the timing of the remaining missing observations is not used for metric-specific adjustment. For contrast only in this first explanation, the primary dataset could be interpreted as a time-sensitive primary metric dataset ; hereafter it is called simply the primary dataset. Applying the same model and global test to the gap-timing-unaware dataset gave raw global p-values of 0.026 near eye and 0.037 at chest. This supports stability to whether the timing of remaining missing observations is used for metric-specific adjustment. It does not test every possible missing-data mechanism.

text: Activity context The exploratory activity analysis uses the accepted primary placement frames and a normalized hourly diary. A 30-minute observation is retained only when there is exactly one containing diary hour and exactly one eligible mapped activity: Home, Sleep, Public transport/car, Indoor work/home office, or Outdoors/active travel. Missing flags, no selection, multiple selections, and an unspecified “other” selection are not imputed. Autocorrelation sequences restart across gaps created by this filter. section: Placement comparability and analyses not run
text: Placement comparability and analyses not run A scalar near-eye-versus-chest identity plot is not valid for H11. The stored primary fits use different all-available samples, and H11 has no fitted common-sample placement outputs or prespecified scalar reduction of its temporal estimand. The reader report therefore presents separate near-eye and chest curves without implying equivalence or a paired placement difference. Show the R code used for this display paired_assessment |> transmute ( ` Stored common-sample participants ` = .data $ stored_common_sample_participants, ` Stored common-sample participant-days ` = .data $ stored_common_sample_participant_days, ` Fitted common-sample H11 outputs ` = .data $ common_sample_H11_fitted_outputs_available, ` Prespecified scalar temporal estimand ` = .data $ predeclared_scalar_temporal_estimand_available, ` Scalar identity plot applicable ` = .data $ scalar_identity_plot_applicable, Reason = paste ( "The accepted H11 fits use unmatched all-available samples and no" , "common-sample H11 model outputs or prespecified scalar reduction exist." ), ` Closest valid display ` = paste ( "Separate primary near-eye and complementary chest curves without" , "a paired or equivalence interpretation." ) ) |> gt :: gt () |> gt :: cols_width ( Reason ~ gt :: px ( 480 ), ` Closest valid display ` ~ gt :: px ( 480 ) ) |> prep_gt ( font_size = 10 ) Table 18: Assessment of a paired near-eye-versus-chest display Stored common-sample participants Stored common-sample participant-days Fitted common-sample H11 outputs Prespecified scalar temporal estimand Scalar identity plot applicable Reason Closest valid display 112 643 FALSE FALSE FALSE The accepted H11 fits use unmatched all-available samples and no common-sample H11 model outputs or prespecified scalar reduction exist. Separate primary near-eye and complementary chest curves without a paired or equivalence interpretation. The registered hourly geometric-mean specification remains preregistration provenance but is outside and superseded by the author-approved final H11 analysis. It is not an outstanding or unresolved sensitivity. This disposition is recorded in DEV-042 . Other analyses remain outside the accepted result set: a paired common-sample placement analysis, leave-one-site-out refits, an all-zero-inclusive frame that has not been provided, and alternative temporal bases or response families. They could address different robustness questions, but none is necessary to document the provenance of the accepted result and none was silently substituted for the prespecified analysis. section: How to examine or reproduce H11
text: How to examine or reproduce H11 Use the project R 4.6.1 library and run only the H11 entry points in their recorded order. The frozen fitted outputs and source-data files allow the reader report and this preparation record to be rendered without repeating model fits or resampling. Rebuilding scientific artifacts should occur only when an analytical input or approved method changes, and should then produce new hashes and manifests rather than silently replacing accepted evidence. Show the R code used for this display environment |> transmute ( Component = .data $ component, Version = .data $ version, Role = .data $ role) |> gt :: gt () |> prep_gt () Table 26: Recorded computational environment for preparation verification Component Version Role R 4.6.1 Authoritative scientific computation and report rendering Quarto 1.9.37 HTML report rendering dplyr 1.2.1 Data manipulation readr 2.2.0 Typed CSV input and output ggplot2 4.0.3 Reader figures gt 1.3.0 Reader tables mgcv 1.9.4 Stored GAM/BAM fits LightLogR 0.10.3 Approved melEDI symlog display transform patchwork 1.3.2 Multi-panel figure composition The preparation-report manifest records every H11-scoped script, test, scientific artifact, source-data CSV, figure, report source, rendered report, and consequential shared policy file with SHA-256, byte size, producer, and R version. Its own integrity is checked after rendering so that the manifest does not contain a circular self-hash.
